haldighati.title: The Dust of Haldighati
haldighati.hook: Where hooves carved fire into the earth and vows outlived breath.
haldighati.story:
## The Dust of Haldighati — the day Mewar lost a field and kept its king

*The battle of Haldighati is described by the Mughal historians Abul Fazl and Badauni, who was present on the field, and remembered in Mewar through the songs of its bards; the story of Chetak's last leap belongs to that remembered tradition, and this telling says so where it does.*

The sun had not yet cleared the ridges of the Aravallis when the first dust began to rise over the narrow pass of **Haldighati**, north of Gogunda. The rocks there have a strange yellow colour, like crushed turmeric, and it is from that colour that the pass takes its name. On the morning of **18 June 1576**, the air was hot and still, and the yellow earth seemed to be waiting for something. Then, far off, came the low thunder of hooves, the clink of harness and the trumpeting of elephants, and the stillness of the valley broke.

At the head of the men of Mewar sat **Maharana Pratap**, on his horse **Chetak**. His spear rested easily against his shoulder, and his eyes did not move from the open ground beyond the mouth of the pass. Around him were the chiefs of his house and his allies: **Hakim Khan Sur**, the Afghan captain who led the vanguard, the old **Ram Shah Tanwar**, once the raja of Gwalior, with his sons, the **Jhala** chiefs, and **Rana Punja** with his Bhil archers, the sons of the forest who knew every rock and goat-track in those hills.

To understand why these men stood there that morning, one has to go back many years. Pratap was born in **1540**, the eldest son of **Maharana Udai Singh II**, into the Sisodia house that had held Mewar since the days of Rana Hammir and, before that, through the Guhilas, since the age of Bappa Rawal. He grew up among forts and horses, and, the bards say, among the old stories of his grandfather **Rana Sanga**, who had fought Babur at Khanwa with eighty wounds on his body. Riding, spear and sword came to him early. Imagine an old teacher in the courtyard at Kumbhalgarh, putting a sword into the boy's hand and saying, "This is not only a weapon. It is the oath of your fathers." Whether or not those words were ever spoken, it was the lesson Pratap carried all his life.

The world he grew into was changing fast. The young emperor **Akbar** was building an empire across northern India, and one by one the Rajput houses made their peace with him. Amber came first, then others, through marriage and high office at the Mughal court. Mewar would not. In **1567** Akbar laid siege to **Chittor**, and in **February 1568** the great fortress fell after a jauhar and a last charge that Mewar never forgot. Udai Singh had withdrawn to the hills before the siege and lived on to rule from them, building his new city of Udaipur by the lakes.

When Udai Singh died in **1572**, Pratap was crowned at Gogunda. Akbar sent envoy after envoy to him: Jalal Khan Qorchi, then **Raja Man Singh** of Amber, then Man Singh's father Bhagwant Das, and finally Todar Mal. Each was received with courtesy, and each went home without the submission the emperor wanted. Mewar's tradition remembers Pratap telling his court that Mewar would be no one's fief. The history is simpler and harder: he would not go to Agra, and he would not send his son in his place. So in 1576 Akbar sent an army against him, under the command of Man Singh, with **Asaf Khan** beside him.

Badauni, who rode with that army, wrote that it was about five thousand horse. Pratap's force was smaller, perhaps three thousand horsemen, with the Bhil bowmen in the hills on either side. The Mughal army had war elephants, musketeers and the discipline of an imperial host. Among its officers were Rajputs of Amber and other clans who had accepted Akbar's service, so that, on both sides of that field, men of the same blood faced each other.

As the dust thickened, Pratap rode a little way along the line. "There is no turning back today," he told the men nearest him, as the bards imagine it. "Let every blow carry the honour of Mewar." The answer came back from a thousand throats: "**Jai Eklingji!**"

Then Mewar charged. Hakim Khan Sur and the vanguard burst out of the pass and struck the Mughal front with such force that it broke. Badauni himself admits that the imperial advance guard and its left wing gave way and fled, some of them for miles. For a time it seemed that the narrowness of the ground and the fury of the first rush would carry the day. Dust rose so thick that, as one account says, it was hard to tell friend from enemy, and the sun itself grew dim.

Pratap rode straight for the centre, where **Man Singh** sat on his war elephant. Here the bards tell their most famous scene. Chetak, the blue-grey horse, reared up and set his forefeet on the elephant's head, and Pratap thrust his spear at the man in the howdah. The spear killed the mahout, but Man Singh ducked behind the iron of the howdah and lived. As Chetak came down, the bards say, the blade fastened to the elephant's trunk cut deep into his hind leg.

Battles are not won by one charge, however brave. The Mughal reserve came up behind the broken front, and a rumour spread through the imperial ranks that Akbar himself had arrived with fresh troops. The fleeing men turned and came back. The great elephants of both sides met in the middle of the field, and Mewar's champion elephant, **Ramprasad**, was captured; Badauni records that it was later sent to the emperor. Slowly, through the heat of the afternoon, the men of Mewar were pushed back towards the pass.

By then Pratap was wounded, and the chiefs who had stood around him were falling. Ram Shah Tanwar died there with his sons, and so did many of the best swords of Mewar. It was then that **Jhala Man**, the chief of Sadri, did what the bards would sing of for centuries. He took the royal parasol and the insignia of the Maharana and rode with them into the thick of the fighting, so that the enemy would take him for the king. "Maharana," his companions said to Pratap, "Mewar needs you alive. The war is not finished." For a moment, the story says, pain crossed Pratap's face. Then he turned his horse. Jhala Man fought on under the royal parasol until he was cut down.

What happened next is pure tradition, and Mewar holds it as dearly as anything in its history. Chetak, bleeding from the leg, carried his master out of the valley with Mughal horsemen behind them. They came to a small stream, and the wounded horse gathered himself and leapt it. On the far side, near the village of **Balicha**, Chetak's strength gave out at last. Pratap knelt beside him in the dust. "Chetak," he said, and his voice broke. The horse opened his eyes once more and was still. A small memorial, **Chetak's chhatri**, still stands near the spot. The bards add another tale, that Pratap's estranged brother **Shakti Singh**, who was with the Mughals, rode after him and, at the sight of the dying horse, gave his own horse to his brother. Historians are doubtful of this, but it is part of how Mewar remembers that evening.

The Mughals held the field, and the next day they marched into Gogunda. But Man Singh did not pursue Pratap into the hills, and Badauni writes that Akbar was displeased with his generals. They had won the battle and failed in its purpose. The Maharana was free, and as long as he was free, Mewar was not conquered.

After Haldighati the war changed its nature. It was no longer fought in open battle but in the hills, the forests and the dark. Akbar himself came to Mewar in the autumn of 1576, and Mughal garrisons were placed at Gogunda, Udaipur and Kumbhalgarh, which fell in 1578. Pratap divided his men into small bands. The Bhils became his scouts and his guides, carrying warnings from hilltop to hilltop. Whenever a Mughal column moved, it was attacked without warning, its supplies were seized, and the attackers vanished before an answer could be made. "This war will not be won on a battlefield," Pratap tells his chiefs in the story. "It will be won by patience." Those years were hard for the royal family too, and later legend tells of bread made from grass and of nights spent in caves. Tradition also says that the minister **Bhamashah** placed his family's wealth at Pratap's feet, so that the war could go on.

The turning point came in **1582**, at **Dewair**, in the hills north of Kumbhalgarh, where a Mughal post held the passes. This time it was Mewar that chose the ground. Pratap and his son **Amar Singh** fell on the post, and the battle cry of the hill people rang out: "**Har Har Mahadev!**" The bards say that Amar Singh drove his spear through the Mughal commander, **Sultan Khan**, and through his horse as well. Whatever the exact truth, Dewair broke the chain of Mughal outposts in that region, and one after another they began to fall.

After 1585 Akbar's attention turned to the north-west, and the pressure on Mewar eased. Pratap recovered most of his kingdom, from Kumbhalgarh to the south, and made a new capital at **Chavand** in the southern hills. Only **Chittor** and the country around **Mandalgarh** stayed out of his reach. The fortress of his fathers remained an unfinished dream.

Time left its marks on him. In the winter of **1597**, at Chavand, Pratap lay dying, still only fifty-six. Tradition says he called Amar Singh to his side and asked him never to let Mewar bow. "We may lose," the story has him say, "but we must not bow." On **19 January 1597** his breathing slowed and stopped, and a silence settled over the hills of the Aravallis.

The dust of Haldighati is still there today, the same yellow earth below the same ridges. It holds the memory of a battle that the empire won and of a king who walked away from the field to fight on for twenty years. It holds the memory of Jhala Man under the stolen parasol, of the Bhil archers in the rocks, and of a wounded horse that would not stop running. However the chroniclers recorded that day, the people of Mewar have always told it the same way: the emperor took the field, but the Maharana kept his kingdom's soul.

## Remembered for

- **The battle of 18 June 1576.** Maharana Pratap's army met the Mughal force of Man Singh and Asaf Khan in the pass of Haldighati, near Gogunda.
- **The first charge.** Hakim Khan Sur and the vanguard of Mewar broke the Mughal front before the imperial reserve restored the line.
- **Jhala Man's sacrifice.** The chief of Sadri took up the royal insignia and drew the enemy onto himself so that Pratap could escape.
- **Chetak's last leap.** Tradition says the wounded horse carried Pratap across a stream before dying near Balicha, where his memorial stands.
- **A victory without its prize.** The Mughals held the field but never captured Pratap, and Akbar was displeased with his commanders.
- **Dewair and the recovery of Mewar.** From 1582 Pratap and Amar Singh won back most of the kingdom, ruling from Chavand until Pratap's death in 1597.

chittor-pyre.title: Embers over Chittor
chittor-pyre.hook: When steel failed, the flames rose higher than any invading banner.
chittor-pyre.story:
## Embers over Chittor — the night of 1568 when the fortress chose its own fire

*The siege of Chittor in 1567–68 is described in detail by Akbar's historian Abul Fazl, while the deeds of Jaimal, Patta and Kalla live on in the songs and traditions of Mewar and Marwar; where the bards go beyond the chronicles, this story says so.*

Night had not yet left the hills when the first flame rose into the sky above **Chittor**. In the courtyards inside the fortress, wood had been piled high and soaked with ghee, and sandalwood had been laid among it. A strange fragrance hung in the cold February air, holy and terrible at once. Down on the plain, the campfires of the imperial army burned in a great ring around the rock, a ring that had tightened day by day for four months. That night there were two fires at Chittor: the one the enemy had lit around the fortress, and the one the fortress had chosen for itself.

Chittor was never just a fort. For eight centuries, since tradition says **Bappa Rawal** took it from the Mori rulers, it had been the heart of Mewar and the seat of the Guhila and Sisodia kings. It had suffered before. In **1303** the Sultan of Delhi, **Alauddin Khalji**, had taken it after a long siege, and the bards remembered a jauhar then. In **1535** **Bahadur Shah** of Gujarat had stormed it, and **Rani Karnavati** had led the women into the fire. Each time the fortress had fallen, and each time Mewar had come back to it. The people of Mewar spoke of Chittor the way one speaks of a living ancestor.

This time the enemy was the Mughal emperor **Akbar**, young, restless and determined to bring every Rajput house under his authority. Amber had already joined him. **Merta**, the land of the Mertiya Rathores, had been taken in 1562, and its chief, **Rao Jaimal Rathore**, had come to Mewar with his followers and been given a place of honour by **Maharana Udai Singh II**. When Akbar marched on Chittor in the autumn of **1567**, the attack was not only against a fortress. It was against the one great Rajput house that still refused to come to his court.

Udai Singh called his council. The chiefs knew that the imperial army had siege engineers, miners and heavy guns, and that a long siege could swallow the whole royal family in one stroke. On their advice the Maharana withdrew with his heirs into the hills to the west, where he had already begun to build a new city by the lake of Pichola, the city that would become **Udaipur**. Saving the dynasty, the council said, mattered more than saving any one fort. But Chittor would not be left empty. Its defence was given to two men.

The first was **Jaimal**, the Rathore of Merta, a seasoned commander who knew every trick of siege warfare. The second was **Patta**, of the Chundawat Sisodias of Kelwa, a young man whom the bards make only sixteen, with fire in his eyes. With them were some eight thousand Rajputs and many thousands of ordinary people from the countryside, who had come up the rock for shelter. The story imagines the two men standing on the ramparts as the imperial tents spread across the plain. "Now this fort will be saved only with our lives," Jaimal says. Patta lifts his sword: "Then our lives are ready."

Akbar arrived before Chittor in late October 1567 and drew his lines around the hill. His engineers began two kinds of work at once. They dug mines towards the foot of the walls, and they built a *sabat*, a great covered approach of timber and earth, wide enough, Abul Fazl says, for elephants to walk inside and high enough for a horseman to ride with his spear upright. Day after day the workers pushed it forward under fire from the walls, and many of them died.

From the ramparts the Rajputs answered with arrows, matchlocks and stones. When a section of wall was battered down by day, the defenders rebuilt it by night. Behind every breach, it seemed, there were men waiting. The cry went up along the walls, "**Har Har Mahadev!**", and every assault was met.

In the middle of **December** the miners were ready. Two mines had been dug beneath the bastions, and the imperial troops stood waiting to rush the breach. The first mine went off, a part of the wall came down, and the soldiers surged forward into the dust. Then the second mine exploded under them. Abul Fazl writes that a great many of the emperor's own men were killed, and that stones and bodies were thrown far across the plain. In the smoke, Jaimal and his men came down into the breach with their swords, and the gap was held.

The siege dragged on through the winter. Food grew short inside the fortress, and so did powder. The sabat crept closer. Then, on the night of **22 February 1568**, Jaimal was on the wall, supervising the repair of a breach by torchlight. Akbar, a fine marksman, was watching from his own battery. He raised his favourite musket, which he called *Sangram*, and fired at the figure moving among the torches. The ball struck Jaimal in the leg. Abul Fazl, who was proud of his master's shot, says the wound was mortal. Mewar's tradition says that Jaimal was not finished yet.

Within hours the decision was made inside the fortress. There would be no surrender, and no one would be taken alive. Abul Fazl records that fires were lit in three places, in the houses of Patta, of Rathore Sahib Khan and of Ishar Das Chauhan. In the imperial camp, men saw the glow and wondered what it was. **Raja Bhagwant Das** of Amber, who stood beside the emperor, knew. "It is the jauhar," he said. "The Rajputs will come out at dawn."

Inside, the women of Chittor gathered around the fires. They had taken off their ornaments and wiped their foreheads clean. There were no tears, the bards insist, only a strange calm. A mother kissed her daughter's forehead and said, "This is not the end. This is how we keep our honour." Then, one by one, holding hands, they stepped into the flames, and the sky over Chittor turned red. The bards say that Patta's mother and his young wife did not enter the fire. They put on armour, took up spears and rode out to die fighting beside the men. Whether or not that happened exactly as sung, Mewar has never forgotten the women of Patta's house.

At the gates the men made ready. They put on saffron robes, the colour of the final battle, and marked their foreheads with tilak. Jaimal could not stand on his wounded leg. Here the tradition tells one of its most famous scenes. His young kinsman **Kalla Rathore** lifted him onto his own shoulders, and so the two went into battle as one warrior with four arms, Jaimal swinging his sword from above while Kalla fought below. Patta looked at them and smiled. "After today," the story has him say, "no one will ever see us defeated." Jaimal answered, "Today we become immortal."

At first light on **23 February** the gates opened, and the last charge came down the slope with the cry "**Jai Eklingji!**" The imperial army was already moving in through the breaches, with war elephants in the lead. For a time, in the narrow lanes and among the temples, the fighting was terrible. The Rajputs fought as men who had nothing more to lose, because that was the truth. Patta fell near the gate that still bears his memory; the Mughal accounts say he was killed in the press of the elephants. Jaimal and Kalla fought until they too were cut down, and the place where Kalla fell is honoured to this day.

When the sun was fully up, it was over. The fortress had fallen. But the victory was a grim one. Angered by the long resistance and by the support the country people had given to the defenders, Akbar ordered a general killing of those who had taken refuge in the fort. Abul Fazl gives the number of the dead as about thirty thousand. The courtyards were full of ash, and there was no joy in that silence.

Even the victor could not forget the men who had held him off for four months. Akbar is said to have had statues of Jaimal and Patta, seated on stone elephants, set up at the gate of his fort; a century later the French traveller **François Bernier** saw two such elephants with their riders at the gate of the Mughal fort at Delhi and was told they were the two heroes of Chittor. Whatever their exact origin, the enemy had honoured the defenders in stone.

Chittor was no longer a living capital. Udai Singh never returned to it, and his court settled in Udaipur by the lakes. But the story did not end there. From those ashes came a new resistance, and its face was that of Udai Singh's son, **Maharana Pratap**, who would fight Akbar's armies for the rest of his life and who, tradition says, swore not to sleep on a bed or eat from gold and silver plates until Chittor was free again.

That night at Chittor did not only end a siege. It gave birth to an idea that Mewar carried for generations: that some defeats are not truly defeats, and that some fires do not go out. Even today, when people walk along the broken walls of Chittor and pass the cenotaphs of Jaimal, Patta and Kalla, they do not only see stone. They remember a fire in which lives were lost, and in which honour, as the bards say, became immortal.

## Remembered for

- **The siege of 1567–68.** Akbar besieged Chittor from October 1567 until its fall on 23 February 1568, while Maharana Udai Singh II withdrew to the hills to save the dynasty.
- **Jaimal and Patta.** Rao Jaimal Rathore of Merta and the young Patta Chundawat of Kelwa led the defence and died in the final battle.
- **The mines of December.** The imperial mines brought down part of the wall, but a second explosion killed many of Akbar's own soldiers and the breach was held.
- **The third jauhar of Chittor.** On the night of 22 February the women of the fortress chose the fire rather than capture, as their ancestors had done in 1303 and 1535.
- **Kalla and the four-armed warrior.** Tradition says Kalla Rathore carried the wounded Jaimal on his shoulders into the last fight.
- **Honour from the enemy.** Akbar is said to have raised statues of Jaimal and Patta on stone elephants at the gate of his fort.

jaipur-lancers.hook: Lances lowered against the impossible, riding straight into history.
jaipur-lancers.story:
## Charge of the Lancers — Rajputana's horsemen at Haifa, 1918

*The charge at Haifa on 23 September 1918 is recorded in the war diaries and official histories of the Palestine campaign; the soldiers' words in this story are imagined, but the ground, the regiments and the outcome are those of history.*

The night had been cool, and the ground along the river was soft and dark. Mud clung to the horses' hooves and made them heavy. Dawn had barely spread across the sky when the men were already standing by their mounts, checking girths and stirrups, speaking in low voices in the Marwari of their villages. In their hands were lances: long shafts of bamboo with steel points, the weapon of another age. Ahead of them, on the slopes of a mountain they had never seen before, lay an enemy with machine guns and artillery. And yet, that day, the attack was to be made on horseback.

These men were the **Jodhpur Lancers**, the *Sardar Risala* of the state of Marwar. In their veins ran a tradition of horse and sword that went back many centuries, to the riders of the Rathores who had fought in the deserts and hills of Rajputana. Swift attack, the sudden charge, breaking an enemy before he could recover: that had always been the way of their ancestors. "The horse is our strength, and our soul too," the old men of their villages used to say.

But the times had changed. After the great rebellion of 1857, the princely states of Rajputana had become allies of the British Crown, keeping their thrones but not their freedom in war and foreign affairs. In **1889**, under a scheme for **Imperial Service Troops**, several states raised small modern forces that could serve beside the Indian Army. Jodhpur raised its lancers under the great soldier-statesman **Sir Pratap Singh**, a son of the ruling house of Marwar. Bikaner raised its famous camel corps, the **Ganga Risala**. Jaipur raised a **transport corps**, whose carts and ponies carried supplies on campaigns from the North-West Frontier to the wars beyond the sea. The flags and uniforms were new, but when the men put them on, the old pride woke inside them.

Then came the First World War, a war that cared nothing for borders or traditions. In 1914 the Jodhpur Lancers sailed for France. Sir Pratap Singh, then nearly seventy, insisted on going with them. For three hard years they served on the Western Front, in the rain and mud of Flanders and northern France. There, cavalry had little place. Again and again the horsemen were held behind the lines, waiting for a breakthrough that never came, and often they went into the trenches on foot, as infantry, with rifles instead of lances. Many of them died far from home, in a cold land without desert or Aravalli.

In 1918 the Indian cavalry regiments were moved from France to Egypt and Palestine, where the British were fighting the Ottoman Empire. There, at last, there was space for horses. The Jodhpur Lancers joined the **Mysore Lancers** and the **Hyderabad Lancers** in the **15th (Imperial Service) Cavalry Brigade**. In **September 1918** General Allenby launched his great offensive at Megiddo. The Ottoman front broke, and the cavalry poured through the gap, riding north across the plains of Palestine faster than the enemy could fall back.

On **23 September** the brigade was ordered to take the port of **Haifa**. The town lay between the sea and the long ridge of **Mount Carmel**. The approach from the east ran along a narrow strip of ground, with the slopes of Carmel on one side and the river **Kishon**, with its marshy banks, on the other. On the mountain the enemy had placed field guns and machine guns that covered the whole approach. The defenders were Ottoman soldiers, with German and Austrian gunners among them. Anyone who rode down that strip of ground would be riding into crossfire.

The plan was simple and dangerous. The Mysore Lancers would climb onto the slopes of Carmel to attack the guns from the flank. The Jodhpur Lancers would charge straight along the valley towards the town. They were led by **Major Dalpat Singh Shekhawat**, a young officer from a Rajput family of Marwar who had already won honour in France.

That afternoon the order came. For a moment there was silence along the line. The story imagines a young sowar turning to the man beside him. "Brother, this is no longer a war for horses." The other smiles faintly. "We are horsemen all the same." Then the call rings out: "Lancers, advance!"

The horses began to move, first at a walk, then at a trot, and then at a full gallop. Mud flew from their hooves. The ground shook. The lances came down together, hundreds of points levelled in one direction, a scene from an older world riding into a modern one.

The first shots came from the slopes. Then the machine guns opened, and the air was full of bullets. Shells burst among the horsemen. Horses fell, and riders were thrown into the mud. Then the leading squadrons reached the riverbank and found that the ground there was not what it seemed. The banks of the Kishon were soft, and in places like quicksand. Horses sank to their bellies, and some could not be pulled free.

The squadrons did not stop. Instead they swung away from the river and charged straight up the lower slopes of Mount Carmel, at the machine guns themselves. It was the kind of decision that cannot be ordered in advance. It is made in a heartbeat by men who know that to halt under fire is to die. "Do not stop!" someone shouted. "Straight on!"

The lancers rode over the gun positions. They speared the machine-gun crews where they stood and cut down those who tried to run. One gun after another fell silent. Somewhere in that charge Major Dalpat Singh was hit and fell, mortally wounded. **Captain Aman Singh Jodha** took command and led the regiment on. Below them, the remaining squadrons swept along the road and galloped into the streets of Haifa itself, while the Mysore Lancers came down from the mountain with the captured guns behind them.

Within about an hour, the fighting was over. The town was in the hands of the brigade. More than thirteen hundred prisoners had been taken, together with field guns and machine guns. For a force of cavalry armed with lances, charging guns on high ground, it was an astonishing result, and the brigade's own losses were remarkably light. Military historians have often called it one of the last great cavalry charges in the history of war.

When the dust settled, the field was strange and quiet. Fallen horses lay on the slopes, and broken lances lay in the grass. Among the dead were their own men, and among them was Dalpat Singh. The story imagines a young lancer sitting alone near the river, still holding his lance. "We won," he says softly. But there is no joy in his voice.

For these men, the charge was nothing new in spirit. Obey the order. Hold the line. Never let the standard fall. They had been taught that from childhood, in the courtyards of their villages and the stables of their chiefs. The flag above them in 1918 was not their own, but their honour, as they understood it, still was. Dalpat Singh was remembered by his regiment and his people as the **Hero of Haifa**, and the men who fell were buried in the war cemetery there, far from the sand of Marwar.

The war ended in November of that year. But the story of those horsemen did not end with it. In **New Delhi**, a memorial was raised to the three regiments of the brigade, the bronze figures that became known as **Teen Murti**, and in 2018 the crossroads where they stand was renamed **Teen Murti Haifa Chowk**. The Indian Army's **61st Cavalry**, the heir of the old state lancers, still marks **23 September** as **Haifa Day**. In Haifa itself, the graves of the Indian soldiers are still tended.

That charge was also the end of an age. For centuries the horse had been the king of war in Rajputana. Now it was giving way to the machine gun, the tank and the aeroplane. Within a few years, the cavalry of the world would be dismounted for ever. But on that September afternoon below Mount Carmel, the horsemen of Rajputana showed that a tradition does not live only in its weapons. It lives in the courage of the people who carry them.

Today, when one looks back at that moment, one sees more than a battle. One sees a final ride, a final clash, a final cry. The horses are running, the lances are lowered, and for a moment time seems to stand still. The old spirit of Rajputana, which had ridden out from Chittor and Mehrangarh, rode out one last time against the modern world, and it did not turn back.

## Remembered for

- **The Imperial Service Troops.** From 1889 the princely states of Rajputana raised their own forces, including the Jodhpur Lancers, Bikaner's Ganga Risala and Jaipur's transport corps.
- **Service in France.** From 1914 to 1917 the Jodhpur Lancers served on the Western Front, often fighting on foot in the trenches.
- **The charge at Haifa.** On 23 September 1918 the Jodhpur and Mysore Lancers took Haifa from Ottoman, German and Austrian defenders, charging machine guns on the slopes of Mount Carmel.
- **The Hero of Haifa.** Major Dalpat Singh Shekhawat fell leading the charge, and Captain Aman Singh Jodha carried it to the town.
- **A last great cavalry charge.** The action is often described as one of the final successful cavalry charges in the history of war.
- **Teen Murti and Haifa Day.** The brigade is honoured by the Teen Murti memorial in New Delhi, and 23 September is still marked as Haifa Day by the Indian Army.

padmini-mirror.title: The Queen in the Mirror
padmini-mirror.hook: A single glimpse turned marble halls into a theater of war.
padmini-mirror.story:
## The Queen in the Mirror — Padmini, Ratansen and the siege of 1303

*The siege of Chittor by Alauddin Khalji in 1303 is real history, recorded by the poet Amir Khusrau, who rode with the Sultan; the story of Padmini, the mirror and the palanquins comes from Malik Muhammad Jayasi's poem* Padmavat *of 1540 and from the Rajasthani ballads and bardic tales that followed it, and this telling keeps it framed as legend.*

That morning the surface of the lake was perfectly still, as if time itself had paused. A light chill hung in the air. In an open pavilion of the palace at **Chittor**, where the carved stone seemed to speak with the ripples of the water, a mirror had been set up. It was no ordinary mirror. In its polished face, the legend says, one saw more than a face. One saw a fate. And in that mirror, for a single moment, a reflection appeared: the reflection of **Rani Padmini**. It was not only beauty. It was a spark that would set an emperor's heart on fire and bring an army to the gates of the most famous fortress in Rajputana.

To tell her story, the bards begin far away, across the sea, in the island kingdom of **Singhal**, which the poets identify with Sri Lanka. There, they say, lived a princess named **Padmavati**, whose beauty was spoken of in every port of the southern seas. Jayasi's poem tells of a wise talking parrot, **Hiraman**, who belonged to the princess and who one day flew away and was sold in the markets of India. The parrot came at last to Chittor, to the court of its king, **Ratansen**, and there it spoke of Padmavati until the king could think of nothing else.

In the poem, Ratansen leaves his throne, dresses as a wandering yogi and sets out with his companions across the sea to win her. After many trials he reaches Singhal, faces danger and the anger of her father, and is finally married to Padmavati, who returns with him to Chittor. In the Rajput telling she becomes **Padmini**, the queen of Chittor. Her beauty was spoken of far and wide, but those who knew her said that deeper than her beauty were her wisdom, her resolve and her calm. When Ratansen looked at her, the story says, he did not see only a lovely face. He saw a companion who could share the fate of his fortress.

Behind the legend stands a real king and a real siege. At the very beginning of the fourteenth century, Chittor was ruled by the Guhila king **Ratnasimha**, the historical figure behind the Ratansen of the poems. He had come to the throne only a short time before, around 1302. In Delhi sat **Alauddin Khalji**, the most ambitious Sultan the city had yet seen. He had already taken Gujarat and Ranthambore, and in the winter of **1303** he marched against Chittor.

The news reached Chittor that the Sultan was coming. His army was vast, and his ambition, the people said, was vaster still. In the legend, it was not the fortress alone he wanted. Rumour said that he had heard of the queen of Chittor and wanted Padmini for himself. In the royal assembly a heavy silence fell. "We will not surrender," Ratansen said in a firm voice. "Chittor will not bow." Padmini looked at him, and there was no fear in her eyes. "Then," she said, "we must be ready for every ending."

At the end of **January 1303** the Sultan's army surrounded the hill. A sea of tents stretched as far as the eye could see. Amir Khusrau, the great poet of Delhi, was in the camp, and he wrote that the Sultan's own tent was pitched between two rivers below the fort. The siege engines, the great stone-throwers called *manjaniqs*, were set up and began to hurl rocks at the walls. Day after day the fortress was pressed a little harder. But the walls of Chittor still stood.

Here the legend takes its most famous turn. One day an envoy came up the hill with a message. The Sultan, he said, would raise the siege and go home in peace if he were allowed only to see the queen. A wave of anger ran through the assembly. "This is an insult!" one chief roared. But Padmini spoke calmly. "Let him see," she said, "but in the way that we choose."

In the version that Rajasthan tells, a pavilion beside the water was made ready, and a mirror was placed in such a way that the Sultan, seated in one room, might see the queen's reflection without ever looking upon her in person. Jayasi's poem sets the scene differently, at a feast and a game of chess, when the Sultan glimpses her face in a mirror for a moment. Either way, the meeting is the same. The Sultan came up into the fortress as a guest, with desire in his eyes and confidence in his heart. He was led inside. Then he looked into the mirror and saw her. For a moment, time stopped. In that reflection, the legend says, he did not see a woman. He saw something he meant to possess at any cost, and in that moment the war was decided.

Deceit, the bards say, is the deadliest weapon of politics. As a courteous host, Ratansen escorted the Sultan down to the gate of the fortress. There the Sultan's men seized him, and the king of Chittor was carried off as a prisoner into the camp below. When the news reached the palace, there was turmoil. Some chiefs wanted to attack at once; others said all was lost. Padmini alone stayed calm. "We will bring him back," she said.

Now two warriors step into the story: **Gora**, an old and seasoned chief, and his young nephew **Badal**, said to be only twelve. In the Rajasthani ballads, above all the *Gora Badal Padmini Chaupai* of the poet Hemratan, they are the heroes of what came next. A message was sent to the Sultan: the queen would come down to him, with her maids and her household, in a train of palanquins, if she might first say farewell to her husband. The Sultan agreed.

So the palanquins came down the hill, seven hundred of them, the bards say, each carried by bearers. But inside each palanquin sat not a maid but an armed Rajput, and the bearers too were warriors in disguise. When they reached the camp and the curtains were drawn back, swords flashed out. "**Har Har Mahadev!**" The Rajputs fell upon the guards, and in the confusion Ratansen was freed and carried back up the hill to safety. Gora died in the fighting at the gate, covering the retreat. Badal, the boy, returned alive, and when Gora's wife asked him how her husband had fought, he told her that he had fought like a lion, and she went proudly to join him on the pyre.

But now war was certain. The Sultan, furious at the trick, pressed the siege harder than before. Month after month the stones fell. The walls began to break, food grew short, and water was rationed. In the legend, Ratansen had already died of his wounds or in battle, and at last the moment came when a choice had to be made.

Padmini entered the assembly. There was no fear on her face. "There will be no surrender," she said. "We will decide our own fate." There was such strength in her voice that no one spoke against her.

That night, the fire pits were made ready inside the fortress. The women gathered, and no one wept; there was only a strange calm. Padmini stood at the very front. She looked one last time at the fortress, at the walls within which her life had passed, and then she walked towards the fire. One by one, all the others followed her. The flames rose, and the sky above Chittor turned red. This was the first of the three great jauhars that Chittor would remember.

Meanwhile the men made ready for the last battle. They put on saffron robes, marked their foreheads with tilak and took up their swords. "Today is the final battle," said one warrior. Another answered, "And to the last breath." Before morning the gates of the fortress opened, and a roar went up: "**Jai Eklingji!**" Then they charged down into the Sultan's army. They fought as men who were already dead, because that was the truth. One by one they fell, and none turned back.

History records the end more briefly. Amir Khusrau writes that the fortress fell on **26 August 1303**, after a siege of about seven months, and that the Sultan ordered a great slaughter of the people inside. Alauddin gave Chittor to his young son **Khizr Khan** and renamed it **Khizrabad**. Khusrau says nothing of Padmini, and historians have long debated whether she ever lived, or whether the poets made her from the memory of the siege and the jauhar. But within a few decades the Guhila line under **Rana Hammir** had won Chittor back, and Mewar never forgot what had happened there.

Padmini was gone, but her choice lived on. The moment of the mirror, when a single glance began a war, became one of the best-loved stories in all of India. Even today, when people stand on the ramparts of Chittor and look down at the palace by the water that is called **Padmini's palace**, they feel a faint warmth in the air, as if the fire has not quite gone out. The guides still show the room where, they say, the Sultan saw the reflection. In the stories of Rajputana, Padmini is no longer only a queen. She is a flame, and a mirror in which the land still sees itself.

## Remembered for

- **The siege of 1303.** Alauddin Khalji besieged Chittor from January to August 1303, a siege recorded by Amir Khusrau, who was present.
- **The legend of Padmini.** The story of the queen from Singhal comes from Jayasi's poem *Padmavat* of 1540 and the Rajasthani ballads that followed it.
- **The glimpse in the mirror.** Tradition says the Sultan was allowed to see only Padmini's reflection, and that this glance sealed the fate of Chittor.
- **Gora and Badal.** In the ballads, the old warrior and his young nephew freed Ratansen by hiding soldiers in palanquins.
- **The first jauhar of Chittor.** The women of the fortress, led in legend by Padmini, chose the fire rather than capture.
- **A memory that outlived the conquest.** Chittor was renamed Khizrabad, but Mewar won it back and kept Padmini's story alive for seven centuries.

kesari-oath.title: The Oath at Dawn
kesari-oath.hook: On cold stone, a sworn promise weighed heavier than any crown.
kesari-oath.story:
## The Oath at Dawn — Kesari Singh Barhath, a poem of warning and a family of rebels

*The verses of Kesari Singh Barhath and the lives of his son Pratap and brother Zorawar are part of the recorded history of India's freedom struggle; the dawn gathering in the courtyard and the words spoken there are imagined, and where tradition goes beyond the record this story says so.*

It was the hour before dawn, when the night has not quite gone and the day is not yet born. The sky was a pale, washed blue. A cold desert wind struck the stone walls and swept through the courtyard of an old house, rattling a shutter somewhere and stirring the ash in a brazier. One by one, men were gathering there, turbans on their heads and woollen shawls around their shoulders, with a gravity in their eyes. No one raised his voice. No one laughed. They only waited. In the middle of the courtyard stood a low platform, and on it lay a folded sheet of paper. It looked like nothing at all. But inside it, the story says, there was a storm.

When the last of them had arrived, one man stepped forward. He was **Kesari Singh Barhath**, a poet and scholar of the **Charan** community, born in **1872** in the little state of **Shahpura**, between Mewar and Ajmer. For centuries the Charans had been the poets, genealogists and counsellors of the Rajput courts. It was their duty to sing the deeds of kings, and also their right, by old custom, to warn a king to his face when he strayed from the path of his ancestors. Kesari Singh's eyes were calm, but a fire burned behind them. Slowly he unfolded the paper, the silence deepened, and he began to read.

It was not merely a poem. It was a warning, and every line cut like the edge of a sword. "Do you not remember the oath of your ancestors?" His voice was low, but it reached every heart. "Will you bow the head that has never been bowed?" For a moment, it seemed, even the wind stood still.

To understand those words, one has to understand the age in which they were written. By the end of the nineteenth century the wars of Rajputana were long over. The princely states had kept their thrones as allies of the British Crown, but the real decisions were made by British Residents and political agents. The kings had palaces and titles, salutes of guns and seats of honour, but not freedom. The struggle was no longer fought with swords on a battlefield. It was fought inside the mind.

In **1902** the Viceroy, **Lord Curzon**, announced a magnificent durbar at **Delhi**, to celebrate the coronation of **King Edward VII** as Emperor of India. It was to be held on **1 January 1903**. The princes of India were summoned from every corner of the land to ride in procession and pay homage. Among them was the ruler of the proudest house of all: **Maharana Fateh Singh** of **Mewar**, the heir of Bappa Rawal, of Rana Sanga and of Maharana Pratap. No Maharana of Mewar had ever stood in an emperor's court to make obeisance. Now the invitation came with a place already set for him, and behind the courtesy lay a demand: to admit, before all of India, that power now belonged to someone else.

When Kesari Singh heard that the Maharana was preparing to go, something broke inside him. "Will Rajputana now be only a spectator at its own humiliation?" he asked himself. The same blood ran in Mewar's veins that had boiled at Haldighati, the same blood that had seen the fires of Chittor. He took up his pen, and the words came. He wrote thirteen short verses in the Dingal language of the bards, in the old form called *soratha*, and gave them the title ***Chetawani ra Chungatya***, "the goads of warning". Each verse was short. Each one was an arrow. They reminded the Maharana that his forefathers had never bowed to Delhi, that Pratap had eaten bread made of grass rather than submit, and that history and his ancestors would never forgive him if he went.

In the story's courtyard, the men who heard the verses felt a wave rise within them. A boy stepped forward. He was Kesari Singh's own son, **Pratap Singh Barhath**, then only a boy of about ten, named after the great Maharana, with fire in his eyes. "Father," he asks in the story, "will this be enough?" Kesari Singh looks at him. "This is only the beginning," he says. "Sometimes words strike deeper than the sword."

The verses travelled quietly, through trusted hands, and reached the Maharana while he was on his way to Delhi. The story imagines him alone in his railway carriage with the paper before him. Line after line pulled him back towards his past. He saw his ancestors on horseback, swords raised, never bowing. What is certain is what he did next. Maharana Fateh Singh went to Delhi, but when the great durbar met on 1 January 1903, he did not take his place. His chair in that vast arena stood empty, and he returned to Udaipur without paying homage. It was not just a decision. It was a message, an empty chair that silently challenged the whole durbar.

But the story did not end there. It had only begun. In the years that followed, the Barhath family moved from words to deeds. Kesari Singh, his younger brother **Zorawar Singh Barhath** and, as he grew older, his son Pratap became part of the secret revolutionary networks that were spreading across northern India. Their links ran to Delhi, to Punjab and to Bengal, and at the centre of one of those networks stood the Bengali revolutionary **Rash Behari Bose**.

On **23 December 1912**, the new capital of British India was celebrated with a state entry into Delhi. The Viceroy, **Lord Hardinge**, rode through **Chandni Chowk** on a great elephant, in a silver howdah, surrounded by every display of imperial power. In the crowd that lined the street were some eyes that were not merely watching. They were waiting. A moment, a signal, and then a bomb was thrown into the howdah. The explosion shook the street. The Viceroy was badly wounded, and the attendant holding the parasol above him was killed. The elephant stood frozen in the smoke while the crowd ran screaming.

The courts later convicted the young **Basant Kumar Biswas** of throwing the bomb, and he and three of his comrades were hanged. But family tradition and many later accounts place **Zorawar Singh** and **Pratap Singh** among the plotters in Chandni Chowk that day. Whatever their exact part, both were now deep in the war of shadows, where every step put a life at risk. Zorawar escaped the police and lived underground for the rest of his life, wandering under other names until his death in 1939.

Every revolution has its price, and now that price began to fall due. In **1914** Kesari Singh himself was arrested in **Kota** and tried on charges of conspiracy and sedition. He was sentenced to twenty years and sent to the distant jail at **Hazaribagh** in Bihar. His pen was taken from him, but his words had already flown. The family's lands were seized, and his household was scattered.

Pratap Singh, still in his early twenties, was arrested for his part in the revolutionary plans of 1915 and sentenced in the **Benares Conspiracy Case**. He was held in the Central Jail at **Bareilly**. There, the police tried day after day to make him name his comrades. He was tortured, and he did not speak. Tradition remembers an officer telling him that his mother was weeping for him, and Pratap answering that he would rather his own mother wept than that a thousand other mothers should. Not a single name left his lips. On **24 May 1918**, worn down by the torture, he died in his cell. He was barely twenty-five years old.

The story imagines a moment in that prison, when a fellow prisoner asks him, "Did we do the right thing?" And Pratap, with a faint smile, answers, "We did what our ancestors would have done."

Kesari Singh was released around 1920, after some six years behind bars, an older and grieving man who had lost his son. He spent the rest of his life writing, teaching and working for the public causes of Rajputana, and he died in Kota on **14 August 1941**, six years before India became free.

Something had changed in the meaning of the old Rajput word for honour. Once, loyalty had been owed to a king. Now, in the lives of the Barhath family, it was owed to the land and to its people, to a new idea called India. The bards of old had warned kings not to bow. Their descendants now warned an empire that a whole nation would not bow.

The courtyard where the verses were first read, in the story, is empty now, but its echo remains in every stone. The men of this family did not raise swords. Yet they too fought a war, with words, with ideas and with their lives. In Shahpura today their memory is kept with pride, and the state of Rajasthan honours them among its heroes of the freedom struggle. The warriors of Haldighati, the flames of Chittor and the empty chair at Delhi are all chapters of the same story. Wars change and weapons change, but whoever refuses to bow is never truly defeated.

## Remembered for

- **The Chetawani ra Chungatya.** In 1903 Kesari Singh Barhath wrote thirteen Dingal verses urging Maharana Fateh Singh of Mewar not to bow at Curzon's Delhi Durbar.
- **The empty chair.** The Maharana travelled to Delhi but stayed away from the durbar of 1 January 1903 and returned to Udaipur without paying homage.
- **The Delhi bomb of 1912.** Zorawar Singh and Pratap Singh Barhath are linked by tradition to the attack on Lord Hardinge in Chandni Chowk on 23 December 1912.
- **Kesari Singh's imprisonment.** Arrested in 1914, he was sentenced to twenty years and held at Hazaribagh until his release around 1920.
- **Pratap Singh's silence.** Tortured in Bareilly jail, he refused to betray his comrades and died there on 24 May 1918.
- **A new meaning of honour.** The family's sacrifice carried the old Rajput ideal of refusing to bow into India's struggle for freedom.

unnamed-sentry.title: The Nameless Sentry
unnamed-sentry.hook: A lone silhouette on the ramparts, holding the night together.
unnamed-sentry.story:
## The Nameless Sentry — the watchman who held the night together

*This is not the story of one recorded man but of thousands whose names were never written down; the night it describes is imagined, set within the real world of the desert forts, their trade routes and their enemies.*

It was the hour of the night when the darkness is heaviest. Far out in the **Thar**, beyond the last of the Aravalli hills, a single figure walked along the rampart of a desert fort. The cold wind tugged at his shawl and filled the folds of his turban with fine sand, but his steps were steady. Below him there was only sand, grey under the starlight, and beyond the sand there was nothing but uncertainty. His name was never written in any chronicle. Yet on his staying awake that night, a whole stretch of the kingdom depended.

The great forts of the desert are famous: **Jaisalmer**, the golden fortress of the Bhatis, raised on its ridge in the twelfth century; **Bhatner**, on the old road from the north-west, which had seen Timur's army in 1398; **Mehrangarh** of the Rathores, rising sheer above Jodhpur; and **Junagarh** in Bikaner. Beyond them stood hundreds of smaller strongholds, thanas and garhis whose names have been lost in the dust of time. But the story of every one of them was the same: high walls, narrow gates, and on those walls, through every hour of every night, a sentry.

He kept walking slowly, his eyes trying to pierce the darkness. Then, far off among the waves of sand, a faint light flickered. He stopped and looked harder. A caravan camped late? A shepherd's fire? Or something else? Without thinking, his hand went to the hilt of his sword.

The wars of Rajputana were not fought only on the great battlefields that the bards sing of. A great deal of the real struggle took place here, on ramparts like this one, in the eyes of nameless watchmen. A kingdom of the desert lived or died by its roads. For the Bhati rulers of Jaisalmer, the tracks across the Thar were not empty borderlands but the arteries of trade. Caravans of camels moved between **Sindh** and the cities of the Ganga plain and Gujarat, carrying cloth, spices, dried fruit, salt and, in later centuries, opium. The tolls they paid filled the treasuries of the desert kings, and the merchants who travelled with them built the carved havelis of Jaisalmer. With the caravans travelled danger: bandits, raiders from beyond the border, rival chiefs, and sometimes whole armies. "If the caravan is safe, the kingdom lives," an old man of the fort had once told the young sentry, and so, every night, there was a watch.

To the north, on the borders of Bikaner and Marwar, tension blew in the wind along with the sand. The Rajput states of the desert were often at odds with one another over wells, villages and grazing grounds, and a moment's carelessness could see a border village raided or a herd of cattle driven off before dawn. On every wall of every fort, therefore, one pair of eyes was always open.

In the south, in the hills of **Sirohi**, the **Deora Chauhans** looked down from their forts onto the valleys and passes around **Mount Abu**. For two centuries the **Sultans of Gujarat** watched those hills from the south, and in the eighteenth century Maratha horsemen swept across Rajputana demanding tribute, followed in their turn by the roving bands of the **Pindaris**. In every age the enemies changed, but the sentry did not. Somewhere in the middle of all of it, there was always that one man on the wall.

That night something in the air felt different. The soldier stopped again. The distant light was growing. It was not one light now, but several, and then many, moving in a line. His heart began to beat faster. "Torches," he muttered under his breath. Shepherds do not carry torches in a line across the open desert at midnight. Caravans halt and sleep. Only men who wanted to arrive before the morning moved like that.

In an instant he made his decision. He ran along the rampart to the great bronze bell that hung by the gatehouse, seized the rope and pulled with all his strength. The clang rang out over the sleeping fort, again and again. Lamps were lit. Men stumbled from their quarters with their swords in their hands. A chief came running up the steps, still fastening his belt.

"What is it?" he demanded.

"Riders, from the west," the sentry said, pointing into the dark.

"How many?"

"I cannot tell yet. But the line is growing."

The orders rang out across the courtyard. "Close the gates! Archers to the walls! Wake the horsemen!" Within moments, the fort that had been asleep was ready for battle. Bows were strung, the great beams were dropped across the gates, and in the stables the horses stamped and snorted as their riders saddled them in the dark.

Outside, horses were racing across the sand towards the walls, a line of torches bobbing above them. They were a band of raiders who had chosen this night because they believed the fort would be sleeping, and that by dawn they would be gone with the herds and grain of the villages below the walls. They were wrong.

As they came close, a rain of arrows fell on them from the battlements. The first volley broke their charge. Horses reared and fell, torches tumbled into the sand, and men shouted in confusion. "Back! Fall back!" their leader yelled. But it was already too late. The small gate in the side of the fort had swung open, and the horsemen of the garrison were already out, riding hard around the walls to fall on the raiders' flank.

The fight that followed was small, but fierce. Swords clashed in the darkness, horses collided, and men fought by the light of fallen torches burning on the sand. It did not last long. Within a short while the raiders had broken and fled back into the night. A few lay where they had fallen. The villages below the walls were untouched, and the fort was safe.

Slowly the morning came. The sky grew pale, then gold. The horsemen rode back through the gate, and the fort went about its business: water was drawn, fires were lit and bread was baked. The sentry stood at his post on the rampart again, as if nothing had happened. When his watch ended, another man would take his place, and he would sleep a few hours before he climbed the steps again the next night.

No one would ask his name. No song would be sung for him. No chronicle would remember him. And yet, if he had fallen asleep that night, a caravan might have been plundered, a village burned, a herd driven off, or a border quietly moved. The great stories of Rajputana, the sieges and the charges and the jauhars, have their heroes. This story has only him.

There were thousands of sentries like him, of every clan, Rathore and Bhati, Hada and Chauhan, Kachhwaha and Sisodia, and many who were not Rajputs at all. There were Bhils in the Aravallis who carried warnings from hill to hill, and Meenas and Charans and herdsmen who knew every track of the desert. They stood on every wall of every fort, on every border, in every century.

The forts tell their own stories of such men. At Mehrangarh, they say, a watchman once saw torches approaching through the night and raised the alarm in time to save the city below. At **Taragarh**, the star fort high above **Bundi**, the Hada garrison tells of a sentry who spotted an enemy column moving in the dark and spoiled a surprise attack. Whether these are memories of real nights or the kind of tale that every fort tells about itself, no record can say. But they are true to the life of those walls.

Then the times changed. The British came, the old wars of the desert ended, and borders were drawn on maps and fixed by treaty. But the watch did not end. When **Maharaja Ganga Singh** of Bikaner raised his famous camel corps, the **Ganga Risala**, at the end of the nineteenth century, its riders patrolled the same desert, with the same vigilance and the same sense of duty. Camel-mounted patrols still watch over the sands of the Thar today.

Many of the old forts are ruins now. Their walls are broken and their ramparts are empty, and the great bells are silent or gone. But if you stand on one of those walls just before dawn, when the sky is turning from black to blue and the wind comes cold off the sand, you may feel that someone is still there: a shadow at the corner of your eye, a figure still walking slowly and carefully along the parapet, looking out into the dark.

Dawn is about to break. And that sentry is still awake. He knows something the chronicles often forget: that history is not always made by battles. Sometimes it is made simply because someone did not fall asleep.

## Remembered for

- **The unseen guardians.** Countless nameless sentries kept watch on the walls of Rajputana's forts through every night of every century.
- **Guarding the caravan roads.** The desert forts protected the trade routes between Sindh, Gujarat and the Ganga plain on which kingdoms like Jaisalmer depended.
- **A single warning.** In this tale one watchman's bell wakes the fort in time to drive off a night raid before it reaches the villages.
- **Every clan and community.** Rajputs of every clan, Bhils, Meenas and herdsmen all stood watch, carried warnings and guarded the borders.
- **The watch continued.** Bikaner's Ganga Risala carried the same vigilance into the modern age, patrolling the Thar.
- **History made by wakefulness.** The story honours those who were never named but without whom the famous battles could not have been fought.

tale-of-pabuji-rathore.title: Tale of Pabuji Rathore
tale-of-pabuji-rathore.hook: The protector of cattle who chose an oath over a crown.
tale-of-pabuji-rathore.story:
## Tale of Pabuji Rathore — the protector of cattle who chose an oath over a crown

*Pabuji's story lives in the oral epic sung by the Bhopa priests of Rajasthan before the painted scroll called the phad, and in the traditions of Marwar; very little of it can be checked against written records, and this telling follows the epic as it is sung while saying where history is uncertain.*

It was a desert night, deep, still and full of mystery. The sky, crowded with stars, seemed to lean down to hear every story of the earth. In a village square in Marwar, a long cloth was unrolled and tied between two poles. In the light of an oil lamp, its colours came alive: red and yellow, green and black. Horses ran across it, swords flashed, gods and heroes stood in rows. This was the **phad**, the painted scroll of Pabuji. Before it stood the **Bhopa**, the singer-priest, with his bowed fiddle, the *ravanhattha*, and beside him his wife, holding the lamp up to each scene in turn. The villagers sat on the sand in a silent ring. Then the Bhopa drew his bow across the strings, and a voice rose into the night: "Listen. This is the tale of Pabuji Rathore."

Pabuji was born, the singers say, on the hard land of Marwar, where every breath was won by struggle. Historians place him, if he lived, probably in the fourteenth century, in the years when the Rathores were still a small, scattered clan in the desert, long before Rao Jodha built Mehrangarh. His father was **Dhandhal Rathore**, a chief of **Kolu**, a village in the dunes north-west of where Jodhpur stands today, and his line went back to **Rao Siha**, the ancestor of the Rathores of Marwar.

The epic gives him a marvellous birth. His mother, it says, was a heavenly nymph who married Dhandhal on one condition: that he never enter her chamber unannounced. One day he broke his word and saw her, in the form of a lioness, nursing the infant Pabuji. She left the world of men that day, but promised to return to her son one day as a mare. So, from the very beginning, the singers say, Pabuji was more than an ordinary prince. It was as if the land had brought him not merely to live, but to do something extraordinary.

While he was still small, a wooden sword was placed in his hand. It was not play. It was training. "A Rajput's word," his teacher told him, as the story goes, "is greater than his life." Pabuji said nothing that day, but the light in his eyes was already a vow. As he grew, the horse's back became his home, the sword his language and honour his dharma. Around him gathered a band of loyal companions, who appear beside him in every phad: **Chando** and **Dhebo**, fierce brothers who would follow him anywhere; **Harmal**, the Raika camel-herder; and **Salji Solanki**. His elder half-brother was **Buro**, and his sister **Pema** was married to **Jind Rao Khichi**, the lord of **Jayal**, a man who would become his bitterest enemy.

Then came the mare. Not far from Kolu lived a woman named **Deval**, of the Charan community, the poets and keepers of tradition who were held sacred in Rajput society. Deval owned a herd of fine cattle, and a black mare of wonderful speed named **Kesar Kalami**. Many chiefs wanted that mare, Jind Rao among them, but Deval refused them all. When Pabuji came to her, she saw something different in him. She gave him the mare, and the singers say Kesar Kalami was none other than his mother, returned as she had promised. But she asked one thing in return. "Raiders have their eyes on my cattle," she said. "If ever they are taken, you must bring them back."

Pabuji looked at her. "I give you my word," he said. "Whenever your cows are in danger, I will come." The word had been given, and for Pabuji a word once given was final.

Kesar Kalami was no ordinary horse. Her gait was like the wind, and in her eyes burned the same flame that burned in Pabuji. When she ran, the singers say, the earth itself made way for her. With her beneath him, Pabuji became more than a warrior. He became a protector of the poor and the helpless, of those whose voices no one heard, and above all of the herds on which the people of the desert depended for their lives.

The epic tells another adventure from these years, one that explains why the camel herders of Rajasthan worship him to this day. At the wedding of his niece **Kelam**, Pabuji promised her the finest gift of all: camels, which were then unknown in Marwar. He sent Harmal far to the south, the singers say to the land of **Lanka**, and after many dangers Harmal brought back a herd of she-camels. Since then, the **Raika** and **Rebari** herders have honoured Pabuji as the god who brought the camel to their land and who guards their animals still.

Time passed, and then came the most famous day of all: Pabuji's own wedding. He rode to **Umarkot**, in the desert of Sindh, to marry **Phulvanti**, a princess of the **Sodha** house. The whole palace was steeped in celebration. Drums were beating, women were singing, laughter rang out through the courtyards. The sacred fire was lit, and the bride and groom began the seven circles around it that would make them husband and wife.

Just then a rider came galloping in, dusty and panting. In some tellings it is Deval herself who sends the word; in others her messenger. "Pabuji!" he cried. "Deval's cattle have been seized! Jind Rao Khichi has driven them off!"

For one moment, everything stopped. Pabuji stood beside the fire, the knot of the wedding cloth still tied to his bride's. On one side were his family, his marriage and the honour of the Sodhas. On the other side was a word he had given. Most versions say that the couple had completed only some of the seven circles. Without a word, Pabuji untied the knot and took up his sword. "Where are you going?" someone asked. He gave only one answer: "To keep my word." And then he was gone. The wedding was left unfinished, but a legend had begun.

Kesar Kalami raced across the sand of the Thar, and the dust that rose from her hooves was like a summons to war. Ahead were Jind Rao's men, driving the stolen herd towards Jayal. They were greater in number, but not in courage. Pabuji drew his sword. "Today no one takes what is not his," he said, and there was such certainty in his voice that even the wind fell still.

The clash was swift and merciless. Swords rang, horses collided, and the sand turned red. A raider rushed at Pabuji and hurled a spear; Pabuji ducked, the spear flew past, and the next moment his sword had struck the man down. "Release the cows!" he roared. Jind Rao's men broke and fled, and the cattle were turned back towards Deval's pastures. In the most widely sung version, Pabuji had his enemy at his mercy that day, but spared Jind Rao's life for the sake of his sister Pema, who would otherwise have been made a widow.

That mercy would cost him everything. Jind Rao, shamed and full of hatred, gathered a great force and came again. The final battle was fought at a place the epic calls **Dechu**. Pabuji and his companions fought as they had always fought, but they were few and the enemy many. One by one they fell: Chando and Dhebo, Salji, Harmal and Buro. At last Pabuji himself was struck down, and the epic says that his soul was carried up to heaven, while Kesar Kalami too gave up her life.

The singers end the battle with a quiet scene. Deval comes to him as he lies wounded, with tears in her eyes. "You kept your word," she says. Pabuji smiles faintly. "A word," he answers, "is never left unfulfilled." Then his eyes grow still. Back in Umarkot, Phulvanti, the bride whose wedding had never been finished, followed her husband in death. And years later, the epic says, Buro's son **Rupnath** grew up to avenge his family by killing Jind Rao.

Time passed. Kingdoms rose and fell. The Rathores built Jodhpur and Bikaner, and wars came and went. But Pabuji did not fade. He became something more than a warrior: a **lok devta**, a folk god of Rajasthan, honoured with Gogaji, Tejaji, Ramdevji and Harbhuji among the great protectors of the desert. His shrine at **Kolu** draws pilgrims every year, and herders still call on him when their camels fall sick. A fifteen-foot scroll of his life is painted in the villages of Rajasthan by the Joshi families of **Shahpura** and **Bhilwara**, and the Bhopas carry it from village to village, singing his story through the night.

Even today, when night falls and the phad is unrolled, the same scenes come alive in the flicker of the lamp. Kesar Kalami runs, swords gleam, and a voice rises over the sand: "This is the tale of the warrior who gave up everything for his word." Pabuji Rathore is not only a name. He is a faith and a flame, still burning in every heart that holds a promise above life itself.

## Remembered for

- **A Rathore of Kolu.** Tradition makes Pabuji the son of Dhandhal Rathore of Kolu in Marwar, probably in the fourteenth century.
- **The promise to Deval.** In return for the mare Kesar Kalami, he swore to protect the Charan woman Deval's cattle.
- **The unfinished wedding.** He left his own wedding to the Sodha princess Phulvanti at Umarkot when news came that Deval's cattle had been seized.
- **Bringer of camels.** The epic says he brought the first camels to Marwar, and Raika and Rebari herders still honour him as their protector.
- **Death at Dechu.** After sparing his brother-in-law Jind Rao Khichi, he fell with his companions when Jind Rao attacked again.
- **The phad of Pabuji.** His epic is still sung through the night by Bhopa priests before a painted scroll, and he is worshipped as one of Rajasthan's great folk deities.
