pabuji-and-the-sacred-camels.title: Pabuji and the Sacred Camels
pabuji-and-the-sacred-camels.hook: How the first camels were brought to the sands of Marwar.
pabuji-and-the-sacred-camels.story:
## Pabuji and the Sacred Camels — the promise that crossed the sea

*This tale lives above all in the epic of Pabuji, sung through the night by the Bhopas of Marwar before a painted scroll called the phad, and in the faith of the Raika herders; it is a legend, and where it parts from recorded history, this story says so.*

Night falls quickly in the Thar. One moment the dunes are gold, the next they are blue, and then there is only the dark and the wind moving the sand in small, patient waves. In a village somewhere in Marwar, on such a night, a long cloth is unrolled between two poles. It is painted from end to end with horses, warriors, gods and camels. A lamp is lit in front of it. A man in a red turban lifts a bowed fiddle called the *ravanhattha*, his wife raises the lamp to one figure on the cloth, and the singing begins. The man is a **Bhopa**, a priest-singer of **Pabuji**, and the story he sings will last until dawn.

The hero of the song is **Pabuji Rathore** of **Kolu**, a village in the desert west of Jodhpur. Tradition makes him a son of **Dhandhal**, of the Rathore clan that had settled in Marwar, and places his life in the fourteenth century. The bards add a wonder to his birth: his mother, they say, was a celestial nymph who returned to the heavens when she was seen in her true form, leaving her infant son behind with the promise that she would come back to him as a mare. Whether one believes it or not, it explains why the bards always speak of Pabuji and his black mare, **Kesar Kalmi**, as if they were one being.

Pabuji did not grow up as a great lord. Kolu was a small place, and the leadership of the family passed to his elder half-brother, **Buro**. What Pabuji had was a reputation. He was the man the weak went to when they had been wronged, and around him gathered a band of companions as unusual as he was. There was **Chando** and **Dhembo**, two brothers of humble birth whom the epic remembers as the bravest of all his men. There was **Harmal**, a **Raika**, one of the camel-herding people of the desert. And there were others, Rajput and non-Rajput alike, bound to Pabuji not by caste but by his word.

His mare came to him, the epic says, from **Deval**, a Charan woman revered as a goddess, who owned a herd of cows and feared for them. She gave Pabuji the mare on one condition: that whenever her cattle were in danger, he would ride to save them. Pabuji agreed. In Marwar, the singers say, a promise was not something a man made lightly, and they want their listeners to remember this condition, because the whole epic turns on it.

The story of the camels begins with a wedding. Buro had a daughter named **Kelam**, and she was married, the epic tells us, to **Gogaji Chauhan**, the hero of Dadrewa who is himself worshipped as a deity across northern India. The chronology of the two heroes does not truly fit, for Gogaji is usually placed centuries earlier, but the folk epics of Rajasthan often join their great figures together, and in the song the two are kinsmen by marriage.

At a Rajput wedding, the bride's relatives give gifts, and the gifts are spoken of for years. Kelam's other relatives gave jewels, horses and cloth. When it was Pabuji's turn, he was silent. He was not a rich man, and he had nothing to give that could stand beside the gold of the others. The women of the household laughed. Some of them, the bards say, mocked Kelam to her face: "Your uncle, the great Pabuji, has brought you nothing."

Kelam came to him that evening with tears in her eyes. Pabuji listened. Then, the singers say, he made her a promise in front of everyone. "I will give you a gift that no one in Marwar has ever given," he said. "I will bring you she-camels, from **Lanka**."

To the people of the desert in the song, Lanka is not the island of the maps. It is the far kingdom across the sea where **Ravana** once ruled and where, the epic says, his line still held a herd of camels. No one in Kolu had ever seen such animals. Some in the courtyard laughed again, louder than before. "A man of the sands," one of them said, "who has never seen the sea, will cross it to steal from the house of Ravana?"

Pabuji did not answer them. He went to Harmal. If anyone could find camels and judge them, it was a Raika. He asked his companion to travel ahead to Lanka in disguise, to learn where the herds were kept and how they were guarded. Harmal shaved his head, put on the ochre robes of a wandering holy man, and set out. The singers spend a long time on this journey: the dry country, the green country, the rivers, and at last the shore where Harmal stood and looked at more water than any man of the desert had ever imagined.

When Harmal returned, he brought the news Pabuji wanted. The camels were real. They grazed in great herds in the land of Lanka, guarded by the king's men. Animals with long necks and padded feet, Harmal said, that could walk for days without water, could carry loads that would break a horse's back, and did not sink in the sand.

So Pabuji gathered his companions and rode south. The epic tells of the crossing of the sea in the language of wonder. In some tellings, Kesar Kalmi, the divine mare, leaps across the water; in others the companions cross by boat, through storms and nights of fear. Every version agrees on one moment. Standing on the shore, with the waves breaking white in front of them, one of the companions asked Pabuji whether it was worth the risk for a gift. Pabuji, the singers say, answered: "A promise given in front of the family is not a gift. It is a debt. A Rathore does not die owing a debt."

On the far side, in a land of rain and green, they found the herds. The herdsmen of Lanka saw strangers on horseback approaching and raised the alarm. The king's warriors came out to meet them. The bards do not make this an easy victory. They describe a long, hard fight, in which Chando and Dhembo cut their way through the guards, Harmal drove the herd away from the battle, and Pabuji himself faced the champions of the king. In the end, the epic says, the warriors of Lanka gave way, and the camels were Pabuji's.

Then came the long journey home. The singers like to describe the faces of the villagers as the herd came out of the shimmer of the desert: strange animals, swaying, their heads high above the riders on their horses. Children ran away screaming. Old men stood and stared. And when the camels walked through the deep sand where horses struggled, people began to understand what Pabuji had brought.

Kelam received her gift. In some tellings, Pabuji himself led the camels to her husband's house as a final wedding present, and the women who had mocked her fell silent. Her uncle had kept his word.

The legend says that this was how the first camels came to Marwar. History tells a different story. Camels had been known in north-western India and the Thar for many centuries before the fourteenth century, and they were already used by traders and armies long before Pabuji's time. But the legend is not really a claim about the history of animals. It is a claim about belonging. For the **Raika** and **Rebari** herders, whose whole life was bound to the camel, Pabuji became the one who gave them their animals and who protects them still. When a camel falls sick, many herders still make a vow to Pabuji; when it recovers, they hold a night-long performance of his epic in thanks.

The epic does not end with the camels. Every Bhopa knows that the song is moving towards a death, and the audience knows it too. Pabuji's marriage was arranged with **Phulvanti**, a Sodha princess of **Umarkot**. In the middle of the wedding, during the sacred rounds around the fire, a messenger came running. **Jind Rao Khinchi**, a chief who was Pabuji's own brother-in-law and long his enemy, had driven off the cows of **Deval**, the woman who had given him his mare.

The singers describe the silence that fell over the wedding. Pabuji had completed only some of the rounds. To leave now was to leave his bride at the fire. To stay was to break the promise he had made to Deval. Pabuji stood up, untied the wedding knot, and mounted Kesar Kalmi.

He caught the raiders and won back the cows. But Jind Rao's men were many, and Pabuji's companions fell around him, one after another. The epic says that Pabuji was killed in that last fight, and that Buro died too, and that Phulvanti, the bride who had never finished her wedding, followed him onto the funeral pyre. The tale of how Buro's son **Rupnath** later took revenge on Jind Rao is another song, sung on another night.

At dawn, when the Bhopa reaches the end, the lamp is lowered and the scroll is rolled up. The phad is more than a painting: it is treated as a travelling temple of Pabuji, and some of the old scrolls are kept and honoured for generations. His main shrine stands at **Kolu**, and his worshippers come there from across the desert.

What stays with the listeners is the shape of his life. Pabuji was a minor Rathore of a desert village who never ruled a kingdom. Yet the people of Marwar have remembered him for centuries, because he crossed the sea for a promise to a girl who had been mocked, and left his own wedding fire for a promise to a woman who owned a few cows. In the sway of a camel walking across the dunes, the Raika still see the shape of his promise.

## Remembered for

- **The promise to Kelam.** When his niece was mocked for receiving no wedding gift from him, Pabuji swore to bring her she-camels from distant Lanka.
- **The journey to Lanka.** With his companions Harmal, Chando and Dhembo, he crossed the sea in the legend and won the camels from the guards of Ravana's land.
- **The bringer of camels.** Legend credits him with bringing the first camels to Marwar. Historically, camels were known in the region long before, but the Raika and Rebari herders still honour him as the protector of their animals.
- **Loyalty to Deval.** He left his own wedding to Phulvanti to rescue the cows of Deval, keeping the condition on which she gave him his mare Kesar Kalmi.
- **Death in battle against Jind Rao Khinchi.** According to the epic, he was killed while recovering Deval's cattle, and his bride Phulvanti followed him onto the pyre.
- **The phad of Pabuji.** His epic is still sung by Bhopas through the night before a painted scroll, one of the great living oral traditions of Rajasthan.

devnarayan-epic.title: Devnarayan Epic
devnarayan-epic.hook: An incarnation of Vishnu who rose to protect the innocent.
devnarayan-epic.story:
## The Devnarayan Epic — the avenger born of the Bagdawat line

*Everything we know of Devnarayan comes from the epic sung by the Gurjar Bhopas before the painted phad of Devnarayan, and from the faith of his temples at Asind, Malasari and Demali; it is a sacred tradition rather than recorded history, and this story tells it as such.*

On a winter night in a village of Bhilwara, a canvas more than ten metres long is stretched out between bamboo poles. Its surface is crowded with figures in red, green and yellow: horsemen, queens, fortresses, serpents, gods. In front of it stands a **Bhopa** of the Gurjar community, holding the *jantar*, a stringed instrument with two gourds, and beside him another singer lifts a lamp to light one painted face after another. This is the **phad of Devnarayan**, said to be the longest of all the painted scrolls of Rajasthan, and the epic sung before it can take many nights to finish. Its hero is worshipped by the Gurjars of Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh as an incarnation of **Vishnu**.

The epic does not begin with Devnarayan. It begins a generation earlier, with his father and uncles: the **twenty-four Bagdawat brothers**, sons of **Bagh Rao**. Tradition gives them a noble origin and great wealth in cattle and land, and describes them as generous, warlike and proud. The most famous of them was **Savai Bhoj**, the hero who would become Devnarayan's father. The bards say the brothers were so rich that they gave away gold as others gave away grain, and that their herds covered the hills.

Their downfall, the epic says, came through **Jaimati**, a woman of extraordinary beauty who was married to **Durjansal**, the Raja of **Rann**. In the sacred telling she is no ordinary woman but a form of the goddess herself, come to earth to bring the proud Bagdawats to their end. Jaimati turned her heart towards Savai Bhoj and came to live among the brothers. Durjansal, humiliated, demanded her return. The Bagdawats refused. What followed, the singers say, was a terrible war in which the twenty-four brothers fell one after another. Savai Bhoj died with them. The Bagdawat line was nearly wiped out.

But one hope remained. Savai Bhoj's wife, **Sadu Mata**, was devoted to Vishnu, and the epic tells that the god himself had promised to be born as her son. In the turmoil after the war, the child was born. Tradition places the birth in **1243 CE** (Vikram Samvat 1300), on the seventh day of the bright half of the month of Magh, at **Malasari**, near Asind in present-day Bhilwara. The singers describe a night of strange light, of cattle lowing in the dark, of a lotus in the courtyard pond that opened at midnight.

Durjansal heard that a son of Savai Bhoj had been born, and he understood what that meant. The child would one day come for revenge. So, the epic says, he sent his men to kill the infant. Sadu Mata did not wait for them. Taking the baby, she fled from the land of the Bagdawats and went south to her own father's home in **Malwa**, where the power of Rann could not reach. There, in the safety of his mother's family, the boy grew up. He was named **Devnarayan**, "the god Narayan", because those around him believed that the god had taken human form.

The epic fills his childhood with signs. He tames wild animals with a touch. He cures the sick. Serpents do not harm him; one legend says a cobra spread its hood over the sleeping baby to shade him from the sun. As he grows, the boy asks about his father, and at last his mother tells him the story of the Bagdawats: the twenty-four brothers, the war, the death of Savai Bhoj, and the reason they had fled.

The young Devnarayan, the singers say, listened in silence. Then he said: "The debt of my father's blood is still unpaid. I was born to pay it."

But revenge was only part of his purpose. In the epic, Devnarayan's life is also about justice for the ordinary people. Malwa and eastern Rajasthan in the time of the song are full of petty tyrants: chiefs who take the herders' cattle, who seize the farmers' grain, who mistreat travellers. Devnarayan answers their cries. In episode after episode, a cattle-keeper or a widow comes to him in tears, and he rides out to set things right.

His power comes partly from his companions. Foremost among them is his horse, **Lilagar**, a blue-green steed of divine birth, who appears in every scene of the phad. With him there is the bard **Chhochhu Bhat**, whose role in the epic is to remember, to carry messages and to tell the story. And around him gather the Gurjar herdsmen, who see in him both a kinsman and a god.

In Malwa, the epic tells of his marriage to **Pipalde**, a princess of **Dhar**. The tellings say that she was ill and that Devnarayan cured her, and that her father gave her to him in marriage. With this marriage, Devnarayan gained allies and the standing of a lord, and Pipalde became a figure of reverence in her own right in the cult of her husband.

Then the time came to return. Devnarayan rode north with his followers to the land of the Bagdawats, where the people who had served his father still lived under the shadow of Durjansal. The epic tells how he gathered the scattered followers of the old house, and how villages that had lived in fear came to him with gifts and men.

The battle with Durjansal is the great climax of the epic. The singers describe the army of Rann as vast, with fortified walls and well-armed horsemen, and Durjansal himself as proud and fearless. Devnarayan's force is smaller, made of herdsmen and farmers and the old retainers of his father's house. Before the battle, the epic says, he spoke to them: "We are not fighting for land. We are fighting so that the strong will learn they cannot do as they please."

The battle itself, as the Bhopas sing it, swings back and forth. Arrows darken the sky. The followers of Devnarayan fall, and for a time it seems the army of Rann will triumph as it did against the Bagdawats. Then, at the turning point of the song, the divine nature of Devnarayan is revealed. Light shines from him. Lilagar charges through the ranks of Rann. Durjansal faces him at last, and is killed. The debt of the Bagdawats is paid.

It is worth saying clearly that the Raja of Rann and the war against him are known to us only through the epic. No inscription or chronicle has been found that records them. The figure of Devnarayan may well have grown around a real Gurjar hero of the thirteenth century whose deeds were remembered and magnified over generations, until he became, in the faith of his people, a god. That is how many of the folk deities of Rajasthan came to be.

After the victory, the epic turns quieter. Devnarayan is shown not as a conqueror but as a protector and healer. He settles quarrels, heals cattle and people, and teaches respect for the cow, the herder and the land. The Gurjars came to see in him the guardian of their whole way of life. His shrines are still visited by people who want their animals to stay healthy, and *neem* leaves are offered at his shrines, because tradition holds that he healed with them.

At the end of his earthly life, the epic says, Devnarayan did not die as others do. At **Demali**, near Masuda in the Ajmer region, he left this world and returned to the divine. His temple there is one of the most sacred places of his worship. Others stand at **Savai Bhoj** near **Asind**, the shrine of his father's memory, and at **Malasari**, where he was born. On his birthday in the month of Magh, and at other festivals through the year, great crowds of devotees gather at these places.

The phad remains the heart of his worship. A Bhopa does not simply perform before it; he worships it. When an old phad is worn out, it is not thrown away but respectfully immersed in a sacred lake or river, and a new one is painted and consecrated. In 2011, the Government of India honoured this tradition with a postage stamp showing the phad of Devnarayan.

As dawn comes, the Bhopa draws the long epic to a close. The lamp is lowered. The crowd, which has listened through the night, rises to touch the scroll. To them, Devnarayan is not a figure from a distant century. He is the god who was once born a fugitive child, who grew up far from home, who came back to right a great wrong, and who still rides Lilagar across the hills of Rajasthan to protect the herds and the people who keep them.

## Remembered for

- **The Bagdawat inheritance.** Born, in the epic, to Savai Bhoj and Sadu Mata after the twenty-four Bagdawat brothers fell in their war against Raja Durjansal of Rann.
- **Birth at Malasari.** Tradition places his birth in 1243 CE at Malasari near Asind, and his devotees revere him as an incarnation of Vishnu.
- **Childhood in Malwa.** Carried to safety by his mother to her father's home in Malwa, where he grew up hidden from Durjansal.
- **The avenging of his father.** In the epic he returned with his followers and defeated and killed Durjansal, paying the debt of the Bagdawats' blood.
- **Protector of herders and healer.** He is worshipped by the Gurjars as the guardian of cattle and the healer of the sick, and neem leaves are offered at his shrines.
- **The phad of Devnarayan.** His epic, sung by the Gurjar Bhopas before one of the longest painted scrolls of Rajasthan, was honoured with a postage stamp in 2011.

devnarayan-and-the-gurjar-warriors.title: Devnarayan and the Gurjar Warriors
devnarayan-and-the-gurjar-warriors.hook: The bond of brotherhood that forged a legacy of protection.
devnarayan-and-the-gurjar-warriors.story:
## Devnarayan and the Gurjar Warriors — the brotherhood of the Aravalli hills

*This tale comes from the epic of the Bagdawats and Devnarayan, sung by the Gurjar Bhopas of Rajasthan, and from the memory kept at his shrines; the battles in it are the battles of the song, not of the chronicles, and this story tells them as tradition.*

In the hills of the Aravallis, between Bhilwara and Ajmer, the morning comes slowly. First the ridges turn grey, then pink, and then the light spills down into the valleys where the herders are already awake, driving their cattle out to the grazing grounds. For centuries the Gurjar herdsmen of these hills have sung, around their fires and before the great painted phad, about a time when their people stood together under one leader. That leader was **Devnarayan**, whom they worship as a god, and the song is above all a song about brotherhood.

The story of that brotherhood begins before Devnarayan was born. The epic tells of the **twenty-four Bagdawat brothers**, sons of **Bagh Rao**, who lived in these hills in a time of plenty. They owned vast herds, they were generous to bards and to the poor, and they were bound to one another so closely that the singers say they were like twenty-four fingers of one pair of hands. Whatever one brother promised, all twenty-four kept. When one was insulted, all twenty-four answered.

That loyalty was their glory, and in the epic it was also their destruction. When the eldest of the heroes, **Savai Bhoj**, took in **Jaimati**, the queen of Raja **Durjansal** of **Rann**, none of the brothers would hear of giving her back. Durjansal gathered his forces and made war on them. The song says the brothers fought one after another and fell one after another, none willing to flee while another stood. The herds were scattered. The villages of the Bagdawats were left in fear.

Years later, the son of Savai Bhoj, raised far away in **Malwa** by his mother **Sadu Mata**, came back into the hills. The Bhopas say that the first people to see him were herders on a hillside, and that they knew him at once: a young man on a blue-green horse, **Lilagar**, with the face of their old lord Savai Bhoj and a light in his eyes that was not of this world.

Devnarayan did not come with an army. He came with a few companions and a purpose. The epic shows him going from village to village through the Aravallis, sitting with the elders, listening to the stories of what Durjansal's men had done since the Bagdawats fell. Cattle had been seized. Grazing grounds had been taken. Families that had served the brothers were now treated as enemies.

The bards like to describe one great gathering in a hollow of the hills. Hundreds of people came: Gurjar herdsmen with their staffs, farmers, old retainers of the Bagdawat house, men of other communities who had their own grievances against the powerful. Devnarayan stood on a rock to speak to them. A young herdsman, the singers say, called out the question in everyone's mind: "We are different people, from different villages. What can bind us together?"

Devnarayan answered: "The same wrong has been done to all of you. Let the same justice bind you." And then, more quietly: "My father had twenty-three brothers. Today I have hundreds."

From that day the herdsmen called themselves his brothers. This is the heart of the tale. The brotherhood of the twenty-four Bagdawats, which had died in the war with Rann, was born again in a wider form: no longer a single family but a whole people, joined by loyalty to Devnarayan and to one another.

The singers then describe how the brotherhood learned to fight. These were not trained armies but herders, who knew the hills better than any soldier of Rann. Devnarayan used that knowledge. In the first clash of the song, a column of Durjansal's horsemen came into a narrow valley to punish a village that had sided with him. Devnarayan's men were waiting. The herdsmen, the song says, had gone up the slopes on both sides with slings and bows, while a band of horsemen waited hidden behind a bend in the valley.

When the enemy column was deep inside, Devnarayan gave the signal. Stones and arrows came down from the heights. The horsemen of Rann, crowded in the narrow ground, could not see where the attack came from. Then Devnarayan's riders charged from behind the bend. The column broke and fled back the way it had come. No one in the brotherhood, the singers say, had fought in a battle before that day. By evening they had won one.

The second deed of the brotherhood in the song is the taking of a stronghold held by Durjansal's men, a walled place on a rocky height that had been used to watch over the grazing lands. "We cannot climb those walls in daylight," one of the herdsmen said. Devnarayan smiled. "Then we will not climb them in daylight."

On a moonless night, the epic says, a small band made noise and lit fires in front of the gate, so that the defenders gathered there. Meanwhile, others led by herders who knew a goat-track up the back of the rock slipped round and over the wall where no one was watching. They opened the gate from inside. By dawn the stronghold was in the brotherhood's hands, and the grazing lands below were free.

The Bhopas fill these episodes with detail that changes from singer to singer: the names of companions, the number of enemies, the clever tricks. It is impossible to say whether any of these fights took place as described. What matters in the song is the lesson the herdsmen draw from them: that people who had been scattered and afraid became strong when they stood together.

Then came the great battle, the one the whole epic has been waiting for. Durjansal himself rode out from Rann with his full strength. The singers describe his army filling the plain, the dust rising so high that it hid the sun, the drums of Rann beating like thunder. On the other side stood the brotherhood: herders, farmers and the old men of the Bagdawat house, with Devnarayan in front on Lilagar.

Before the battle, the song says, one of the elders came to Devnarayan with tears in his eyes. He had seen the Bagdawats fall on a field like this one. "Your father and his brothers were braver than any men alive," he said, "and they all died. Why should it be different now?" Devnarayan answered: "Because they fought for their pride. We are fighting for one another."

The battle in the song is long and terrible. The brotherhood is pushed back. Many fall. At the darkest moment, the Bhopas sing, the god in Devnarayan shows itself, and his followers see him shining in the dust like a lamp. They rally around him. Lilagar carries him into the heart of the enemy, and there he meets Durjansal. "You think you are a god?" the Raja shouts. "I am only the servant of what is right," Devnarayan replies. Their swords meet, and Durjansal falls. With their lord dead, the army of Rann breaks and flees.

When the dust settled, the song says, Devnarayan did not claim the throne of Rann or take its treasure for himself. He returned to the hills and to his people. The brotherhood did not disperse. It became a way of life: the herders of the Aravallis looked after each other's herds, defended each other's villages, and gathered at his shrine to remember what they had done together.

That memory lives on. The shrines of Devnarayan at **Savai Bhoj** near **Asind**, at **Malasari** where he was born, and at **Demali** where he is said to have left the world, are places where the Gurjar community still gathers in great numbers. On those nights, when the phad is unrolled and the *jantar* begins, the old men and the young sit side by side to hear again how a scattered people became a brotherhood. And when the wind moves through the valleys of the Aravallis, the herders say it sounds like singing.

## Remembered for

- **The twenty-four Bagdawat brothers.** In the epic, the sons of Bagh Rao were bound so closely that they lived and died as one, falling together in their war with Raja Durjansal of Rann.
- **Return of the son of Savai Bhoj.** Raised in Malwa, Devnarayan came back to the Aravalli hills to gather the scattered followers of his father's house.
- **A brotherhood of a whole people.** He united Gurjar herdsmen, farmers and old retainers into one band, renewing the Bagdawat brotherhood in a wider form.
- **The valley ambush and the night assault.** In the song, his herdsmen used their knowledge of the hills to defeat a column of Rann and to take a stronghold by a secret path.
- **Victory over Durjansal.** The epic ends the war with the death of the Raja of Rann in single combat with Devnarayan.
- **A living tradition.** The Gurjar community still gathers at his shrines at Savai Bhoj, Malasari and Demali to hear the epic sung before the phad.

tejaji-and-the-serpent-vow.hook: A martyr who kept his word even at the cost of his life.
tejaji-and-the-serpent-vow.story:
## Tejaji and the Serpent Vow — the word that was kept to the last breath

*Tejaji's story has come down to us through the folk songs of Marwar, the tejas sung in the fields at sowing time, and the faith kept at his shrines at Kharnal and Sursura; where tradition and recorded history part, this story says so.*

At the start of the monsoon in Marwar, when the first rain has darkened the sand and the farmers go out to plough, a particular kind of song can be heard across the fields. It is called a *teja*, and it is sung to make the work go well and to keep the snakes away. Its hero is **Veer Tejaji**, the folk deity of the Jat farmers of Rajasthan, who are said to have learned from him that a promise is stronger than death. Today his shrines, called *thans*, stand in thousands of villages, and in almost all of them he is shown the same way: a warrior on a horse, with a serpent biting his tongue.

According to tradition, Tejaji was born in **1074 CE** at **Kharnal**, a village in the Nagaur region of Marwar. He belonged to the **Dhaulya** clan of the **Jats**. His father, **Taharji**, was the headman of Kharnal, and his mother's name is remembered as **Ramkunwari**. The songs say that his parents had long prayed for a son and that he was born after many vows to the serpent deities, which is why the snakes would later recognise him as their own.

As was the custom of the time, Tejaji was married while still a small child. His bride was **Pemal**, the daughter of **Raimal**, a Jat headman of **Paner**, a village in the Ajmer region. After the ceremony, the little bride went back to her parents' house, as was usual, to wait until she was old enough for the *gauna*, the ceremony at which a wife is brought to her husband's home. Then a family quarrel broke out between the two households, and the matter was set aside. Tejaji grew up without even knowing that he was married.

He grew into a tall and strong young man, known in Kharnal for his honesty and his skill on a horse. He worked his father's fields and was the first, tradition says, to show the farmers of the region a better way of sowing. His mare was named **Lilan**, and the two were rarely apart.

One day, at the start of the rainy season, his sister-in-law teased him. "You plough and sow like a bachelor," she said, "while your wife waits for you in her father's house." Tejaji was astonished. When he learned the truth, he decided at once to go to Paner and bring Pemal home. His family tried to stop him: the old quarrel was not healed, and the omens, they said, were bad. Tejaji would not be held back. He saddled Lilan and rode south.

On the way, the songs tell, he passed a place where a fire had broken out in the scrub. In the middle of the flames a serpent was trapped, writhing as the fire closed around it. Tejaji did not hesitate. He reached in with the tip of his spear, lifted the snake out and set it down on the cool sand.

The serpent did not thank him. Instead, the songs say, it rose in anger. "Why did you save me?" it hissed. "I had lived out my life and wished to die in that fire, and you have robbed me of my death. Now I will bite you, and you will die in my place."

Tejaji did not draw back. He answered calmly: "I cannot stop you. But I am on my way to fetch my wife, and there may be other duties waiting for me. Let me go. I give you my word that I will return here, and then you may do as you wish." The serpent looked at him for a long moment. Then it lowered its head and let him pass.

At Paner, the welcome was cold. Pemal's mother had not forgiven the old quarrel, and Tejaji was treated with little respect. But **Pemal** herself was overjoyed to see him, and the songs give a tender scene in which the young bride, who had waited all these years, finally meets the husband she barely remembered.

That same night, a woman named **Lachha**, a Gujari cowherd of the village, came running to Tejaji in distress. Raiders had driven off her cows. In the songs they are Meena raiders from the hills. Everyone else in the village was afraid to follow. Tejaji was a guest; this was not his village and not his fight. But Lachha had come to him, and he could not refuse. He promised to bring the cows back and rode out alone after the raiders.

He caught up with them in the hills. The songs describe a fierce fight in which one man fought many. Spears and arrows struck him again and again. He was wounded in his arms, his legs and his chest, but he did not turn back until the raiders broke and fled, leaving the cattle behind. He drove the herd back to Paner. Then Lachha told him that one calf, the favourite of the herd, was still missing. Tired and bleeding, Tejaji rode out once more, found the calf and brought it home.

His body was now covered in wounds. Yet he had not forgotten the serpent. Without resting, he turned Lilan back towards the place in the scrub where he had made his promise. The songs say Pemal begged him to stay, and that he told her: "If I do not keep my word, then my coming here for you means nothing."

The serpent was waiting where he had left it, and, the songs say, it was astonished to see him. It had not believed that any man would come back to his own death. It looked at his body, and there was no place on him that was not torn by a wound. "Where can I bite you?" it said. "Every part of you is already wounded, and I will not strike where blood has already been shed."

Tejaji thought for a moment. Then he opened his mouth and put out his tongue. "This is still whole," he said. "Bite here."

The serpent, the songs say, was humbled. Before it struck, it gave him a blessing: that from that day on, anyone bitten by a snake who took Tejaji's name and tied a thread in his name would be saved. Then it bit him on the tongue, and Tejaji died at **Sursura**, in the Ajmer region. Tradition places his death on the tenth day of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapad, in **1103 CE**. Pemal, the songs say, became a *sati* on his pyre. His faithful mare Lilan carried the news home to Kharnal.

None of this can be checked against the chronicles of the period. Tejaji's dates and deeds are known through tradition, not inscriptions, and the dialogue with the serpent is clearly the stuff of legend. But the story was preserved because it expressed something the farmers of Marwar valued above all: that a person's word, once given, must be kept, whatever the cost.

Tejaji's death made him a deity. His shrines spread across Rajasthan and into Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, and he is worshipped today by people of every caste, not only by Jats. When someone is bitten by a snake, villagers still take them to a Tejaji shrine, where the priest ties a thread called a *tanti* around the wound and calls on the hero's name. On **Teja Dashami**, the anniversary of his death in the month of Bhadrapad, great fairs are held, the largest at **Parbatsar** in Nagaur district and at Sursura, where his temple stands.

The farmers still sing the tejas as they plough. Their words are simple, and their lesson has not changed in nine hundred years: Tejaji did not have to go back. No one would have known if he had not. He went back because he had promised.

## Remembered for

- **Birth at Kharnal.** Tradition places his birth in 1074 CE in the Jat village of Kharnal in Nagaur, as the son of Taharji of the Dhaulya clan.
- **Journey to Paner.** He rode to his in-laws' village to bring home his wife Pemal, who had been married to him in childhood.
- **The promise to the serpent.** After saving a snake from a fire, he promised it that he would return to be bitten once his duty was done.
- **Rescue of Lachha's cattle.** He recovered the herd of the cowherd woman Lachha from raiders, returning even for a single lost calf despite his wounds.
- **The bitten tongue.** Covered in wounds, he kept his word and offered his tongue to the serpent, dying at Sursura, by tradition in 1103 CE.
- **Protector against snakebite.** He is worshipped across Rajasthan as the healer of snakebite, and Teja Dashami is celebrated with great fairs at Parbatsar and Sursura.

gogaji-the-snake-protector.hook: The warrior-saint who rules over the serpent kingdom.
gogaji-the-snake-protector.story:
## Gogaji the Snake Protector — the Jahar Veer of Dadrewa

*Gogaji's life comes to us through the songs of his devotees, the traditions of the Chauhans of Dadrewa and the memory kept at Gogamedi; very little of it can be confirmed from the records of his age, and where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the month of Bhadrapad, when the monsoon has turned the scrub of northern Rajasthan green, long lines of pilgrims walk along the roads towards a small town in the sands of Hanumangarh. They carry yellow flags and long poles decorated with peacock feathers, and they beat drums and sing as they walk. Some have come from Punjab, some from Haryana, some from as far as Uttar Pradesh and Himachal. Hindus and Muslims walk side by side. They are going to **Gogamedi**, to the shrine of **Gogaji**, whom the Hindus call **Jahar Veer** and the Muslims **Goga Pir**, and whom everyone calls the protector against snakes.

According to tradition, Gogaji was a **Chauhan** Rajput, born in the eleventh century at **Dadrewa**, a village in what is now the Churu district of Rajasthan. His father was **Jewar**, a Chauhan chief of the place, and his mother was **Bachhal**. The songs tell that Bachhal was childless for many years, and that she served the great yogi **Gorakhnath** with devotion until he blessed her. He gave her a piece of *guggal*, an aromatic resin, to eat, and from that blessing her son was born. The bards say that the name *Goga* comes from that *guggal*.

The songs fill his birth with wonders. At the moment he was born, they say, lightning flashed across the sky, and snakes came out of their holes all over Dadrewa, not to harm anyone, but as if to welcome a master. As a child he played with serpents as other children play with puppies, and they never struck him. The old men of the village, the songs say, watched him lay his hand on a cobra's spread hood and calm it, and they whispered that this was no ordinary boy. As he grew, he was trained as every Chauhan youth of the border was trained: to ride, to use the spear and the sword, to defend the herds and the wells on which the desert villages depended. The followers of Gorakhnath, the Nath yogis, remained close to the family, and the songs say the boy learned from them too, sitting at their fires and listening to their teaching.

Whatever we make of these tales, there is no doubt about the land into which he was born. The country around Dadrewa was the borderland of the Chauhans, on the edge of the desert, open to the north and west. In the early eleventh century, the armies of **Mahmud of Ghazni** were raiding deep into India from the north-west. His great march to the temple of **Somnath** in Gujarat, in **1025 CE**, passed through the deserts of Rajasthan. Many local chiefs of that region must have faced his forces or the bands that moved with them.

Gogaji's devotees remember him as one of those who stood against the invader. The songs say that when Mahmud's army came through the desert, Gogaji rode out to meet it with his sons and kinsmen, and that he and many of his family fell fighting. Some tellings give the exact numbers of the sons and nephews who died with him. Historians cannot confirm any of this. No contemporary record names Gogaji, and the story of his fight against Mahmud is a tradition, not a documented battle. But the memory is strong, and it explains why, in the songs, he is not only a holy man but a warrior who died defending his people.

The songs also tell of his marriage to **Siriyal**, a princess from a distant land, and of the trials he went through to win her. In one tale, her family would not give her to him until a serpent sent by Gogaji bit her and he alone could heal her. These episodes are the stuff of the epic and change from singer to singer, but they all return to the same idea: the snakes obey Gogaji, and whoever is bitten can be saved in his name.

The best-known part of his story, however, is a family tragedy. Gogaji had two cousins, the twins **Arjan** and **Surjan**, who claimed a share of his lands. They were jealous of him and refused to accept his authority. The songs describe the quarrel growing slowly, as such quarrels do: a disputed field, a boundary stone moved in the night, harsh words at a family gathering. Gogaji tried at first to settle it with patience. "We are of one blood," he is made to say. "What is mine is not worth a brother's life." But the twins took his patience for weakness. In the songs they make war on him and even bring in outside forces against him.

The bards describe the battle on the open sand outside Dadrewa, the dust rising under the horses, the Chauhan banners on both sides, kinsman facing kinsman. Gogaji did not seek the twins out, the songs say, but in the end they came at him together, and he had no choice. He fought them and killed them both.

When he came home, his mother Bachhal met him at the door. The twins were her sister's sons, and she could not forgive the killing of her kin. "Go," she said. "I never want to see your face again."

The songs make much of this moment: the victorious warrior standing in the doorway of his own house, refused by his mother. Gogaji obeyed. He left Dadrewa. But his heart could not bear the exile, the songs say, and he came back secretly at night to see his wife. When his mother discovered it, she was angrier still.

In his grief, Gogaji went out into the desert. He prayed to the earth to take him, since he was not wanted in the world above. Tradition says that he turned to the Nath yogis for guidance and learned the way of the Muslim saints too, so that he is remembered by both faiths. Then, at the place now called **Gogamedi**, he rode his blue horse into the earth, and the ground opened and closed over him. He entered his *samadhi*, the songs say, alive.

This is the end of his story as his devotees tell it, and it is the beginning of his worship. At Gogamedi his tomb became a shrine. The building that stands there today has the shape of a Muslim tomb, with an inscription in the Persian script, while the worship within is shared by Hindus and Muslims. It was rebuilt in later centuries, and Bikaner's rulers are remembered as patrons of the shrine. A second shrine, called the **Shirsh Medi**, stands at Dadrewa, where tradition says his head fell.

Gogaji's cult spread far beyond his own country. Across Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Himachal and Uttar Pradesh, his shrines are found in villages large and small. He is shown riding a blue horse, carrying a spear, with a serpent coiled around him or raising its hood above him. In many places the shrine is simply a clay platform with a carved stone showing a horseman and a snake. People who have been bitten are brought to his shrines, and farmers make offerings to him before the rains, when snakes are most active.

Every year in the month of Bhadrapad, on **Goga Navami**, the great fair is held at Gogamedi. For days, the roads are full of pilgrims. They sing the songs of Jahar Veer, carry his yellow banners, and lay offerings at his tomb. In Punjab and Himachal, devotees carry long poles called *chhari* decorated with peacock feathers and colourful cloth in his honour. Men who are possessed by his spirit, it is said, dance in a trance and are believed to heal those who come to them.

Gogaji's story holds together things that are often kept apart: Rajput and yogi, Hindu and Muslim, warrior and saint. He is remembered as a fighter who defended his land, as a son who obeyed his mother even when it broke his heart, and as a holy man who went into the earth and became the protector of everyone who walks barefoot through the fields where snakes hide. When his devotees call "Jahar Veer Gogaji!" at Gogamedi, they are calling on all of these at once.

## Remembered for

- **A Chauhan of Dadrewa.** Tradition makes him the son of Jewar and Bachhal, born in the eleventh century at Dadrewa in present-day Churu, by the blessing of Guru Gorakhnath.
- **Master of serpents.** From childhood, the songs say, snakes obeyed him, and he is still worshipped as the protector against snakebite.
- **Defender against Mahmud of Ghazni.** His devotees remember him fighting the Ghaznavid invasion of the 1020s. This is a tradition that historians cannot confirm.
- **The tragedy of Arjan and Surjan.** He killed his rebellious twin cousins in battle, and his mother Bachhal banished him for it.
- **Samadhi at Gogamedi.** Tradition says he rode into the earth alive at Gogamedi, where his shrine is honoured by Hindus and Muslims alike.
- **Goga Navami.** The great fair at Gogamedi in Bhadrapad draws pilgrims from across northern India to the shrine of Jahar Veer, or Goga Pir.
