ramdevji-of-runicha.hook: The saint of the marginalized who preached equality and peace.
ramdevji-of-runicha.story:
## Ramdevji of Runicha — the Pir of Pirs who sat with the outcast

*Ramdevji's life comes to us through the hymns called banis, the night-long jammas of his devotees, the traditions of the Tanwar Rajputs and the memory kept at Ramdevra; where tradition and recorded history part ways, this story says so.*

Every year, in the month of Bhadrapad, the desert roads of western Rajasthan fill with people on foot. They come from Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, from Marwar and Mewar, from the cities and from villages too small to appear on any map. Many carry small white or multicoloured flags. Some carry little cloth horses. Along the roadsides, people set up free kitchens and water stalls for them. They are walking to **Ramdevra**, the place once called **Runicha**, in the Jaisalmer district, to the shrine of **Baba Ramdev**. Hindus call him an incarnation of Krishna. Muslims call him **Ramsa Pir**. To the poorest of the poor, who were once kept out of so many temples, he is simply their own god.

According to tradition, Ramdev was born in the fourteenth century, in the house of **Ajmal**, a **Tanwar** (Tomar) Rajput chief of the region around Pokaran in western Marwar. The traditional date of his birth is **1352 CE** (Vikram Samvat 1409), in the month of Bhadrapad, and most traditions place it at **Undu-Kashmir** in the Barmer region. His mother was **Minal De**. The Tanwars of the region traced their descent from the old Tomar rulers of Delhi, who had lost their kingdom to the Chauhans two centuries earlier.

The songs tell that Ajmal and Minal De were long without a son, and that Ajmal made a pilgrimage to **Dwarka** to pray before Krishna. There, in his despair, he is said to have thrown a ball of sweets at the image of the god, asking why his prayers were not answered. That night, the songs say, Krishna appeared to him and promised to be born as his son. Ajmal's first son was **Viramdev**, whom devotees see as Balarama; his second was Ramdev, whom they see as Krishna himself.

The songs fill Ramdev's childhood with miracles. When his mother was boiling milk on the fire and saw it about to spill, the infant reached out and set the pot down. When he asked for a toy horse, the tailor who made it stole the fine cloth and stuffed it with rags, and the cloth horse, the songs say, rose into the air with the child on its back. This is why devotees still offer little cloth horses at his shrines. In another tale, the boy killed a demon named **Bhairav** who had been terrorising the region around Pokaran, and the land, freed from fear, was resettled.

But the deeper story of Ramdev is not in these wonders. It is in the company he kept. The society of fourteenth-century Marwar was bound by strict rules of caste. The people known as untouchable, such as the **Meghwals**, were kept outside the temples and away from the wells of the upper castes. Ramdev, the son of a Rajput chief, ignored these boundaries. He ate with the poor, sat with the sick and the outcast, and welcomed everyone to his gatherings.

The most loved figure among his disciples is **Dali Bai**, a girl of the Meghwal community. Tradition says that she was found as an abandoned baby under a tree and that Ramdev's family raised her. She grew up as his devoted follower and became a saint in her own right. Her shrine stands beside his at Ramdevra.

The songs remember many who came to him in their last hope. One of them tells of an old man, so weak with sickness that he had to be carried, whom the healers of his village had already given up. His family laid him down outside Ramdev's door, afraid even to come in, because they were of low caste. Ramdev came out to them himself. He knelt in the dust beside the old man, put his hand on his forehead and sat with him through the night. By morning, the song says, the old man's breathing had steadied and the light had come back into his eyes. Whether one reads it as a miracle or as the comfort of being cared for, the people who saw it never forgot that the son of the chief had knelt in the dust for one of them. Word of it spread from village to village: a saint had come who treated everyone as equal.

One of the most famous stories of Ramdev concerns five **Pirs**, Muslim holy men who came, the tellings say, from Mecca to test him. They had heard of the Rajput saint who worked miracles and wanted to see if the stories were true. Ramdev welcomed them and invited them to eat. The Pirs said they could not eat, because they had left their own bowls in Mecca and would eat from no other. Ramdev smiled, the songs say, stretched out his hand, and the five bowls appeared before them. The astonished Pirs bowed to him and called him **"Pir of Pirs"**. This is why Muslims know him as Ramsa Pir and honour him as a saint.

The story is a legend, but its meaning is clear. In a time when Hindus and Muslims in the region often kept apart, Ramdev's followers remembered him as a holy man respected by both. His teachings, as preserved in the hymns sung by his devotees, stress that God is one, that all people are equal before Him, and that devotion matters more than birth.

The songs tell of how this teaching angered some. The upper castes of the region complained that he was breaking the rules of society. Some priests, it is said, refused to admit his low-caste followers. Ramdev's answer, the bards say, was to build his own place of worship where all could come. "Wherever true devotion is," he is made to say, "that is the temple."

Ramdev married **Netalde**, a princess of **Amarkot**, whom tradition describes as unable to walk until he healed her. He settled at **Runicha**, which he is said to have founded on land granted to him, and it became the centre of his following. People came there from far and wide to seek healing and to listen to his teaching. The tradition of the *jamma*, a night-long gathering of song in his honour, is said to have begun among his followers there.

His devotees formed a tradition that later came to be known as the **Kamadia** panth, and the singers of this tradition still travel through the villages performing his hymns. Many of the hymns sung in his name are attributed to later poets and disciples, but they all preserve the same teaching of equality and devotion.

The end of Ramdev's life is told with great reverence. In **1385 CE** (Vikram Samvat 1442), according to tradition, he decided to take *jeevit samadhi*, to enter his tomb alive, at Runicha. He was still a young man, about thirty-three years old. The songs say that he gathered his family and followers and told them it was time. Dali Bai, his faithful disciple, asked to go first. She took her own samadhi a day or so before him, beside the place that had been prepared for her master.

Then, the songs say, Ramdev sat down in his samadhi, gave his last blessing to the people around him, and closed his eyes. His followers covered the tomb. The faithful believe that he did not die but remains present there, watching over everyone who comes to him.

His samadhi at Ramdevra became one of the great pilgrimage places of Rajasthan. The temple that stands there today was built in the twentieth century, but worship at the site goes back centuries. The fair held in the month of Bhadrapad, from the second to the eleventh of the bright half, draws vast crowds of pilgrims every year. Near the temple is the **Ramsarovar**, a tank that tradition says Ramdev himself had dug.

What makes his story remarkable is not only the miracles. It is that a Rajput chief's son of the fourteenth century chose to sit with those whom society had pushed outside. In the centuries since, the people who had the least have made his shrine their own. When pilgrims reach Ramdevra after days on foot and cry out "Jai Baba Ramdev!", they are honouring a man who, the songs say, taught that no one is high and no one is low before God.

## Remembered for

- **Birth in a Tanwar family.** Tradition places his birth in 1352 CE as the son of Ajmal and Minal De, and devotees revere him as an incarnation of Krishna.
- **Champion of the outcast.** He ignored the boundaries of caste, sat with the poor and the untouchable, and raised the Meghwal girl Dali Bai, who became his disciple.
- **The Pir of Pirs.** In the legend of the five Pirs from Mecca, he produced their own bowls for them, and Muslims still honour him as Ramsa Pir.
- **Founder of Runicha.** He settled at Runicha, now Ramdevra in Jaisalmer district, which became the centre of his teaching and the tradition of the jamma.
- **Jeevit samadhi in 1385 CE.** According to tradition, he entered his tomb alive at Runicha at about thirty-three, with Dali Bai taking her samadhi beside him.
- **The fair of Ramdevra.** Every year in Bhadrapad, vast crowds of pilgrims of all faiths and castes walk to his shrine.
ramdevji-of-runicha.coverAlt: Ramdevji on his horse, blessed with divine light.

veer-durgadas-rathores-loyalty.title: Veer Durgadas Rathore’s Loyalty
veer-durgadas-rathores-loyalty.hook: The unyielding pillar who saved a dynasty from an empire.
veer-durgadas-rathores-loyalty.story:
## Veer Durgadas Rathore's Loyalty — the man who kept Marwar alive for thirty years

*Durgadas's life is unusually well recorded for a Rajput hero: Marwar's chronicles, Persian histories of Aurangzeb's reign and the letters of the period all speak of him. The bards have added their own colour, and where their songs go beyond the record, this story says so.*

In the winter of **1678**, a messenger rode into Jodhpur with news that froze the fort. **Maharaja Jaswant Singh** of Marwar, one of the greatest nobles of the Mughal empire, had died at **Jamrud**, near the Khyber Pass, where Emperor **Aurangzeb** had posted him to guard the north-western frontier. He had left no living son. His two queens with him in the north were both pregnant, but no one yet knew whether either would bear an heir.

Aurangzeb moved at once. He placed Marwar under direct imperial control, sent Mughal officers into its towns, and in 1679 granted the title of Raja of Jodhpur to **Indra Singh Rathore** of Nagaur, a distant kinsman who paid heavily for the honour. To the Rathores of Marwar, it looked as if their kingdom was being swallowed whole.

Then, in **February 1679**, at Lahore, the two queens gave birth to sons. One of them died soon afterwards. The other, **Ajit Singh**, lived. Marwar had an heir. And the man who would make sure that the heir survived was a Rathore noble of about forty named **Durgadas**.

Durgadas was born on **13 August 1638**, the son of **Askaran Rathore**, a minister in Jaswant Singh's service. The family tradition says his mother lived apart from his father, and that he grew up with her in a village near Jodhpur, working the land and learning to ride and fight. The bards tell how the young Durgadas killed a camel driver of the royal herds who had let his camels trample the family's fields and then insulted the Maharaja's name. When he was brought before Jaswant Singh, he did not deny it. The Maharaja, impressed by his courage and honesty, took him into his service. Whatever the details, he rose in the following years to become one of the most trusted men at the court of Marwar.

In the spring of 1679, the queens and the infant Ajit Singh were brought to Delhi. The Rathore nobles petitioned Aurangzeb to recognise the child as the heir of Jodhpur. The emperor's answer, as the Marwar chronicles remember it, was that the boy should be raised in the imperial household, and that his claim would be considered when he came of age, with hints that he might be brought up as a Muslim. To the Rathores this meant that the child would become a hostage, perhaps lost to them forever. They refused.

In **July 1679**, imperial troops were sent to take the child from the Rathore mansion in Delhi. What followed is the most famous episode of Durgadas's life. The Rathores had prepared. The infant had already been smuggled out, tradition says hidden in a basket of sweets, and another child had been left in his place. The Rathore warriors then fought their way out of the city. While some of their best men, among them **Raghunath Bhati** and **Ranchhordas Jodha**, held the Mughal soldiers back in the streets and lanes, dying where they stood, Durgadas rode with the rest towards Marwar, fighting off pursuers along the way.

The bards turn this flight into a song of heroism, with Durgadas turning back again and again to face the pursuers alone. The truth is grim enough on its own. Many Rathores died in Delhi that day so that the child could escape. Ajit Singh was taken in secret to **Kalindri**, in the hills of Sirohi, and raised there in hiding in the household of a Brahmin, under the guard of **Mukunddas Khichi**. For years only a handful of people knew where he was.

Aurangzeb, furious, sent his armies into Marwar. Jodhpur was occupied. Temples were damaged. The emperor also turned on **Maharana Raj Singh of Mewar**, who had sheltered the Rathores and supported their cause. Marwar and Mewar now stood together against the empire. This was the beginning of the long war that the chronicles call the **Rathore rebellion**, and Durgadas was its heart.

He could not meet the Mughal armies in open battle and hope to win. Instead he fought as the desert allowed. Small bands of Rathore horsemen struck at Mughal outposts, raided supply columns and vanished into the sand. When imperial forces moved in strength, the Rathores melted away into the hills of Mewar or the deserts of the west; when the imperial forces divided, the Rathores came back. The imperial officers never could hold the countryside of Marwar for long.

In **1681**, Durgadas played his boldest card. Aurangzeb's own son, **Prince Akbar**, who was commanding the imperial army against the Rajputs, was persuaded by Durgadas and the Mewar leaders to rebel against his father and claim the throne himself. For a few days it looked as if the empire might be shaken. But Aurangzeb, by a clever trick, sent a forged letter that made the Rajputs believe that Akbar was secretly betraying them. Many of Akbar's supporters deserted him overnight. Durgadas, once he understood the deception, did not abandon the prince. He escorted Akbar across India to the Deccan, to the court of the Maratha king **Sambhaji**, son of Shivaji, a long and dangerous journey through hostile country. Akbar eventually sailed for Persia, where he died in exile.

Akbar left behind two children, a son and a daughter, **Buland Akhtar** and **Safiyat-un-Nissa**, and they came into the care of Durgadas. He raised them with honour. When it came time for the girl's education, he hired a Muslim teacher so that she might be brought up in her own faith and learn the Quran. When at last, in the 1690s, the children were returned to Aurangzeb as part of the negotiations, the emperor is said to have been astonished to find his granddaughter well schooled in her religion. Even Aurangzeb, the bitterest enemy of the Rathores, recognised the man's integrity.

Meanwhile, Ajit Singh grew up. In **1687** he was brought out of hiding and presented to the Rathore nobles, who had fought for him for years without seeing him. The war continued through the 1690s and into the 1700s, with phases of truce and negotiation. Durgadas, at times, accepted a Mughal *mansab* and posts in Gujarat as part of the settlement, without ever giving up the cause of Marwar.

The end came not on a battlefield but with a death. In **March 1707**, Aurangzeb died in the Deccan. As the empire fell into a war of succession among his sons, Ajit Singh moved quickly on Jodhpur, and the Mughal garrison withdrew. After twenty-eight years, the son of Jaswant Singh entered his father's capital. The new emperor, **Bahadur Shah**, eventually recognised him as Maharaja of Marwar.

The bards like to end the story here, with Durgadas quietly leaving the court in his moment of triumph and asking for nothing. The truth was sadder. Ajit Singh, now a grown and proud ruler, grew suspicious of the old general who had made him king, and listened to courtiers who whispered that Durgadas was too powerful. Within a few years of the victory, Durgadas was pushed out of Marwar. He went first to Mewar, where Maharana **Amar Singh II** gave him a home and an estate, and later to **Ujjain** on the Kshipra river.

Durgadas died at Ujjain on **22 November 1718**, at the age of eighty. He was cremated on the banks of the Kshipra, and his *chhatri* (memorial) still stands there. He had spent his whole life serving a family that, in the end, drove him away. He never turned against it.

In Marwar, the people did not forget. In songs still sung across the desert, he is remembered as the ideal of loyalty: a man who served his master's son for thirty years without wanting a throne for himself. A Marwari saying wishes that every mother might bear a son like Durgadas. In the sand dunes and the villages, they say, if one listens carefully, the wind still carries his name.

## Remembered for

- **The rescue from Delhi (1679).** He led the Rathores who smuggled the infant Ajit Singh out of Aurangzeb's capital, while comrades such as Raghunath Bhati died holding back the imperial troops.
- **Thirty years of resistance.** From 1679 to 1707 he led the Rathore war against Mughal rule in Marwar, using the desert and the hills to wear down the imperial armies.
- **The alliance with Mewar and Prince Akbar.** He joined forces with Maharana Raj Singh and in 1681 supported Prince Akbar's revolt, then escorted the prince to Sambhaji in the Deccan.
- **Honour to an enemy's children.** He raised Akbar's son and daughter with care, arranging for the girl to be taught her own faith, which won even Aurangzeb's respect.
- **Restoration of Ajit Singh (1707).** After Aurangzeb's death, the prince he had protected since infancy entered Jodhpur as Maharaja.
- **Loyal in exile.** Pushed out of Marwar by the ruler he had saved, he died at Ujjain in 1718, never turning against the house he served.
veer-durgadas-rathores-loyalty.coverAlt: Durgadas Rathore riding through the Thar desert.

hadi-ranis-sacrifice.title: Hadi Rani’s Sacrifice
hadi-ranis-sacrifice.hook: A queen who gave her head to ensure her husband’s victory.
hadi-ranis-sacrifice.story:
## Hadi Rani's Sacrifice — the bride who sent her head as a token

*The story of the Hadi Rani comes to us through the bardic traditions of Mewar and Hadoti, retold in Rajasthani songs and in modern Hindi poetry. Its core is remembered as history in Salumbar, but its details belong to tradition; where the tellings differ, this story says so.*

In the second half of the seventeenth century, the kingdom of Mewar was ruled by **Maharana Raj Singh I**, who sat on the throne of Udaipur from **1652** to **1680**. It was an age of hard choices. The Mughal Empire under **Aurangzeb** pressed ever more heavily on the Rajput states, and Mewar, which had made its peace with the Mughals only in 1615, watched its old independence grow thin. Raj Singh was a builder and a soldier both, the ruler who raised the great embankment of Rajsamand lake, and he was not a man to bow further than he must.

Among the nobles who stood closest to his throne were the **Chundawats** of **Salumbar**. They descended from **Chunda**, the eldest son of Rana Lakha, who in the fifteenth century had given up his right to the throne of Mewar so that his father's promise to a younger queen's son might be kept. In return, tradition says, his line received the first place among the nobles of Mewar and the honour of leading the vanguard, the *harawal*, in war. The Rawat of Salumbar was the first sword of the kingdom. When Mewar marched, a Chundawat rode at its head.

In the time of this story, the Rawat of Salumbar was **Ratan Singh Chundawat**. He was young, and he had only just been married. His bride came from the **Hada Chauhans** of **Bundi**, the clan that gave its name to the land of Hadoti in the south-east of Rajasthan. The people of Mewar called her simply the **Hadi Rani**, the queen of the Hada clan, and that is the name under which she is remembered. Many tellings give her own name as **Salh Kanwar**.

The bards dwell on those first days in Salumbar. The palace still smelled of marigold and sandalwood. The walls still carried the auspicious marks of the wedding; the henna had not yet faded from the bride's hands, and the songs of the women had barely fallen silent in the courtyard. In the evenings the hills around Salumbar turned blue in the dusk, and the young Rawat, the tradition says, could not bear to be away from his wife for even an hour.

Then a rider came up the road from Udaipur with a summons from the Maharana.

The tellings differ on which war called him. The most common version links it to one of the boldest acts of Raj Singh's reign. **Charumati**, the princess of **Rupnagar** in Kishangarh, had been demanded in marriage by Aurangzeb. She refused, and she sent word to the Maharana of Mewar, asking him to save her honour by marrying her himself. Raj Singh rode to Rupnagar and took her as his bride, an act the emperor could only see as defiance. In this version, Ratan Singh Chundawat was ordered to hold back the Mughal troops on the road, so that the Maharana could carry out the marriage and return. Other tellings set the story in the long war between Mewar and Aurangzeb that broke out in **1679**. The tradition does not fix the year, and this story does not pretend to. What every telling agrees on is that the summons was urgent, that the enemy was powerful, and that the Rawat of Salumbar was expected to lead.

The order was read in the hall of the palace. Ratan Singh heard it in silence. The war drums were beaten in the town below, and the men of Salumbar began to gather: horses saddled, swords taken down from the walls, saffron cloth brought out of chests. Yet the young chief lingered in the women's quarters long after the drums had begun.

The Hadi Rani watched him. She had grown up in the fort of Bundi, among a clan whose men were known across Rajputana for their stubborn courage, and she had heard since childhood what it meant to be the wife of a Rajput chief. She saw her husband take a step towards the door and turn back. She saw him look at her as if he were trying to memorise her face.

"The drums have been beating since morning," she said. "Why do you still stand here?"

"I am going," he answered. "But my heart stays behind."

"Then take your heart with you," she said, "and lay it at the feet of the Maharana. That is where it belongs today."

The tradition says that he did ride out at last, at the head of his men, through the gate and down the road. But the bards say he rode slowly. At some distance from the town he stopped and called one of his trusted retainers to him. He had left his bride without a keepsake, he said; he wanted something of hers to carry into battle. "Go back to the Rani," he told the man. "Ask her for a *sainani*, a token, some sign of her that I can keep with me on the field."

The messenger rode back to the palace. The Hadi Rani heard the request, and the tellings say that she understood at once what it meant. Her husband was not truly asking for a ring or a scarf. He was asking for a reason to look back. A chief who rode into battle thinking of the bride he had left behind would not fight with his whole heart, and a Chundawat who did not fight with his whole heart, at the head of Mewar's vanguard, could lose far more than his own life.

The bards imagine her moment of decision in many ways. In some songs she stands for a long time at the window, looking down at the road her husband has taken. In others she speaks only a few words to her maid. In all of them she is calm. She asked for a platter to be brought and a cloth to cover it. She told the messenger to wait. Then, the tradition says, she took up a sword and struck off her own head, so that nothing of her would remain in this world to hold her husband back.

The maid's cry brought the household running. The messenger, trembling, did what he had been told to do. He carried the covered platter out of the palace, mounted his horse, and rode after his lord.

Ratan Singh was waiting by the roadside. When the messenger arrived, the man could not speak; he only held out the platter. The Rawat lifted the cloth. On it lay the head of the Hadi Rani, the eyes closed, the face calm, the vermilion still bright in the parting of her hair.

For a long moment, the bards say, the world stood still around him. Then the chief who had been unable to leave his wife's side understood what she had done and why. She had set him free. There was nothing left to look back for.

"You have given me your token," he said at last, so the songs tell it. "Now I will give the Maharana mine."

Tradition says he tied the head around his neck by her long hair, so that she would ride with him into battle. Then he turned his horse towards the enemy.

What followed is told in the songs as a storm. The men of Salumbar had seen their chief hesitate on the road that morning; now they saw him ride at the head of the vanguard with no hesitation at all. He threw himself where the enemy was thickest. Each time he struck, the bards say, he called her name. The enemy horsemen, who had expected a delaying skirmish, found themselves facing a man who no longer cared whether he lived. The tellings agree that the enemy was held and driven back, and that the task the Maharana had given to Salumbar was accomplished.

They agree less about how Ratan Singh's own day ended. In some versions he fell on the field, fighting to the last with his bride's head at his breast. In others he survived the fighting, dismounted when it was over, gently unbound the head and held it in his hands, and then, having done his duty to his lord, took his own life so that he might follow her. In all the tellings the victory is a sorrowful one. The bards do not sing of triumph on that evening; they sing of a road, a platter, and a silence.

Historians have no contemporary record of this episode, and the Persian chronicles of Aurangzeb's reign do not mention it. It survives as a tradition of Mewar and of the Hada clan, told in family histories, in folk songs and in the memory of Salumbar itself. In the twentieth century it found new life in Hindi poetry, above all in **Meghraj Mukul**'s celebrated poem *Sainani*, which generations of schoolchildren in Rajasthan learned by heart.

To modern ears the story can be hard to hear. It is a tale of a young woman's death, told as glory. But for the people who first sang it, the Hadi Rani was not simply a victim. She was the one who made the decision. In their eyes she understood the moment better than her husband did, and she chose for herself what she would give. The tradition remembers her not as a wife who obeyed, but as a queen who acted.

In Rajasthan, the name of the Hadi Rani has become a byword for sacrifice and resolve. Her story is retold at festivals and in schools, and in Salumbar, the old seat of the Chundawats, it is told as the town's own. When people speak of someone who placed duty above every comfort, they still reach for her name, and for the image of a covered platter carried down a hill road towards a waiting rider.

## Remembered for

- **The token.** When her husband sent back for a keepsake, tradition says she sent her own head so that nothing would hold him back.
- **A bride of a few days.** She was newly married to Rawat Ratan Singh Chundawat of Salumbar, leader of Mewar's vanguard, when the call to war came.
- **The pride of two clans.** A daughter of the Hada Chauhans of Bundi and a bride of the Chundawats of Mewar, she is honoured in both Hadoti and Mewar.
- **The age of Raj Singh.** Most tellings place her story in the reign of Maharana Raj Singh I (1652–1680), during his conflicts with Aurangzeb.
- **The vanguard held.** The tradition says Ratan Singh fought with her head tied at his neck, and that the enemy was held back.
- **A living tradition.** Her story lives in folk songs, in the memory of Salumbar and in Meghraj Mukul's poem *Sainani*.
hadi-ranis-sacrifice.coverAlt: Hadi Rani offering her head as a sacrifice.

veer-kalyan-singhs-last-ride.title: Veer Kalyan Singh’s Last Ride
veer-kalyan-singhs-last-ride.hook: Charging into the maw of death to protect the sacred soil.
veer-kalyan-singhs-last-ride.story:
## Veer Kalyan Singh's Last Ride — the charge that made an army stop

*The tale of Veer Kalyan Singh is a bardic legend, told around fires and in village squares rather than written in any chronicle. No historian can fix his clan, his year or the name of the enemy he faced. What follows is the tradition as it is told, set against the real customs of Rajput warfare; where the story belongs to legend, it says so.*

The bards begin, as they so often do, with the land. Marwar is a country of sand and thorn, of wells sunk deep into hard ground, of villages that can see a rider coming from miles away. The tradition says Kalyan Singh was born there, in a small village on the edge of the dunes, to a family of Rajput landholders who owned a few fields, a few horses, and a sword that had come down from father to son for longer than anyone could remember. In that country, the singers say, a boy learns to sit a horse before he learns to read, and learns the weight of a sword before he learns the weight of a plough.

Kalyan Singh, they say, was different from the other boys from the start. He was not the strongest of them, nor the loudest. But when the others raced their horses across the open ground, he watched how the ground lay, where the sand was soft and where it was firm, where a rider could turn and where he would founder. When the men of the village talked of old fights, he asked not only who had won, but why.

His teacher in arms, an old retainer of the family whose name the songs do not keep, noticed this. One evening, after a long day of practice with the lance, the old man sat with the boy beside the well and told him the thing the bards always repeat. "War is not won by strength alone," he said. "Strength you will find in many men. War is won by the mind that knows when to use it."

Kalyan Singh said nothing that evening. But the tradition says he carried that sentence with him for the rest of his life, and that everything he did on the battlefield grew from it.

By the time he was a grown man, his name had begun to travel. He was quick with the sword and quicker on horseback, and he had the rare gift of keeping his head when others lost theirs. Like many young Rathores and other Rajputs of the desert country, he went to seek service where his sword was needed. The legend sends him to **Mewar**, the hill kingdom to the south whose rulers had long welcomed warriors from Marwar. Real history knows many such men. When Akbar besieged **Chittor** in 1567–68, the defence of the fort was led by **Jaimal Rathore** of Merta, a Marwar chief fighting for Mewar, and the bards of both lands still sing of him. The tale of Kalyan Singh belongs to that same world, where a man's birthplace and the land he died for were not always the same.

In Mewar, the story goes, he served a chief whose lands lay on the edge of the kingdom. And there, one day, the message came that every border chief dreads: an enemy army was advancing. The legend does not name it. In the songs it is simply "the enemy", vast in number and strong in arms, so many horsemen that their dust hung over the horizon like a second sky.

The chief called his council. The older men sat in a circle on the floor of the hall, and the mood was heavy. Messengers had counted the enemy's tents and returned with numbers no one wished to believe. "We cannot face them in the open," one old chieftain said at last. "We should hold the fort and wait for help from the capital."

Kalyan Singh rose. "If we wait," he said, "they will burn every village between here and the hills before help comes. We will face them."

"But we are few," someone answered.

The bards say a light came into his eyes then. "Battles are not won by numbers," he said. "They are won by resolve, and by striking where the enemy does not expect it. They believe we will hide behind our walls. Let us show them we will not."

It was a desperate plan, and every man in the hall knew it. Kalyan Singh proposed not an ambush in the hills, nor a night raid, but a charge: a single head-on blow by every horseman they had, delivered at first light on open ground, before the enemy had finished forming its lines. The ground he chose was a broad, dusty plain with no cover at all. There would be nowhere to hide and no way to turn back. "Head-on?" one young warrior asked, scarcely believing it. "Head-on," Kalyan Singh replied. "We will not give them time to think."

Such charges were not mere poetry. Rajput warfare had always placed its trust in the shock of cavalry, and history records at least one moment when a small Rajput force nearly broke a far greater army in exactly this way. In **1544**, at **Giri-Sumel** in Marwar, the commanders **Jaita** and **Kumpa** led a few thousand Rathore horsemen in a desperate charge against the army of **Sher Shah Suri**. They were killed almost to a man, but the fury of their attack so shook the victor that a famous remark is attributed to him: that he had nearly given away the empire of Hindustan for a handful of millet. The legend of Kalyan Singh is told in the spirit of such days.

That night the camp did not sleep. Swords were sharpened on whetstones until they sang. Horses were fed and watered and their harness checked strap by strap. Many of the men tied on saffron turbans, the colour of those who do not expect to return. Kalyan Singh walked among them, speaking quietly to each. Then he went to his own horse, a tall desert mare who had carried him since he left Marwar, and stood with his hand on her neck. "Tomorrow," he told her, "we fly."

At dawn the order came. "Charge!"

The horses moved slowly at first, then faster, then at full gallop, hundreds of riders in one line across the open plain. The ground shook beneath them. The bards love this moment and draw it out: the dust rising behind the line like a wave, the lances lowering, the first rays of the sun catching on the blades.

The enemy had not expected it. Its camp was still forming, its horses still being saddled. Officers shouted orders that came too late. The Rajput line struck the front of the enemy army and drove deep into it before any proper defence could be raised. Swords clashed, horses collided, and for a while the plain disappeared in dust.

Kalyan Singh was at the very front. The singers say his sword moved like lightning. One enemy horseman fell, then a second, then a third. Behind him his men cut into the confusion, and for a time it seemed that the impossible might happen and the great army would break.

But numbers, in the end, are numbers. As the sun climbed, the enemy recovered. Fresh squadrons closed in from both sides. The Rajput charge slowed, then stopped, and then each man was fighting for his life in a sea of enemies. A spear struck Kalyan Singh in the shoulder. He tore it out and kept fighting. "Don't stop!" he shouted to those around him. "Forward!"

Around him his companions fell one by one. Each of them, the bards say, had already accepted death the night before, and so none of them turned back. Kalyan Singh was soaked in blood now, his own and others', but the same fire still burned in his eyes. His mare staggered under a blow and kept going. He drove her forward one last time, raised his sword, and brought down another enemy rider.

Then the mare fell. The dust rose around them, and for a moment, the singers say, time itself stood still. Kalyan Singh came down on one knee, his sword still raised. An enemy soldier stepped towards him. "Now it is over," the man said.

Kalyan Singh looked up at him. There was no fear in his face, only the same fire. He struck once more, and the soldier fell beside him. Then, at last, the warrior from Marwar was still.

The bards end the tale with a silence. The field grew quiet. The enemy had won; there was no doubt of it. But, the story says, its commanders did not advance that day. They looked at the plain, at the dead horses and the fallen men in their saffron turbans, at the swathe that a few hundred riders had cut through their army, and they hesitated. If this was how the border fought, what would the heart of the kingdom do? In the legend, the delay gave the kingdom time to gather its strength, and the invasion that had seemed unstoppable faltered.

Whether this happened exactly so, no record can say. But it is the kind of ending the people of Rajputana have always understood. Some battles are not won by surviving. They are won by striking so hard that the victor learns to fear the next fight.

In the villages of Marwar and Mewar alike, the tale of Kalyan Singh's last ride is still told on winter nights. The old men say that when the desert wind blows hard across the open ground at dawn, you can hear in it a single word shouted from the front of a charging line: "Forward!" And the young listen, and remember that the warrior who has already accepted death is the one that even death must respect.

## Remembered for

- **The lesson of the mind.** Tradition says he lived by his teacher's words: that war is won not by strength alone but by the mind that directs it.
- **A son of Marwar in Mewar's service.** The legend makes him a Marwar-born warrior who fought for Mewar, like many real Rathores, among them Jaimal of Merta at Chittor.
- **The dawn charge.** Facing a far larger army, he chose an open, head-on cavalry charge at first light rather than waiting behind walls.
- **Fighting to the last.** Wounded by a spear and unhorsed, he struck down one more enemy before he fell.
- **The army that halted.** The tale says the victors were so shaken that they did not press on that day.
- **The spirit of Giri-Sumel.** His story echoes the real charge of Jaita and Kumpa against Sher Shah Suri in 1544.
veer-kalyan-singhs-last-ride.coverAlt: Kalyan Singh leading his last cavalry charge.

tale-of-the-charan-bards.title: Tale of the Charan Bards
tale-of-the-charan-bards.hook: The keepers of fire who ensured no hero was ever forgotten.
tale-of-the-charan-bards.story:
## Tale of the Charan Bards — the keepers of fire who would not let a hero be forgotten

*The Charans were real people, a community of poets, genealogists and guardians of honour whose verses are among the great treasures of Rajasthani literature. The scene at the heart of this tale, of a bard steadying a wavering king on the morning of battle, is a tradition told of many courts and many battles rather than a single recorded event; where the story passes from history into legend, it says so.*

In the last watch of the night, when the torches on the ramparts had burned low and the smell of horses and iron hung over the camp below, a man stood alone at the edge of the firelight. He carried no sword and no shield. He wore a plain turban and a long robe, and the soldiers who passed him lowered their voices as they went by. He was a **Charan**, and in the land of Rajputana that meant he was a man whom even kings did not lightly cross.

Wars in Rajputana were never fought with weapons alone. They were fought with memory, with pride, with the knowledge of who one's fathers had been and what they had done. The people who kept that knowledge alive were the bards, and among the bards the Charans held a special place. Tradition held them to be sacred, a people under the protection of the goddess, and their persons were inviolable. To harm a Charan was a sin that no Rajput would willingly carry. To be praised by one was a gift beyond gold. To be rebuked by one, in verse, before the assembled court, was a wound that could last for generations.

The Charans were not born to the sword, but their words, the saying went, cut deeper. From childhood a Charan boy learned the long poems of his people: the genealogies of the ruling clans, the deeds of heroes, the stories of sieges and sacrifices, the exact lines in which praise and blame had been given in his grandfather's time and his grandfather's grandfather's. He learned to compose in **Dingal**, the old literary language of the bards of western Rajasthan, with its thundering rhythms and its strict forms, the *doha*, the *soratha* and the *geet*. A Charan did not usually sing to an instrument, as a court musician might. He declaimed. His voice alone was his instrument, and a trained Charan voice could carry across a battlefield.

They were more than poets. Caravans travelling through the desert often took a Charan with them, because robbers feared to attack a party under his protection. Promises made before a Charan were binding, and when a ruler broke his word, a Charan might sit at his gate in protest and, in the most extreme cases, wound himself, shedding blood that the ruler would have to answer for. The Rathores of Bikaner revered **Karni Mata**, a Charan woman of the fifteenth century whose blessing, tradition says, guided **Rao Bika** when he founded his kingdom in **1488**, and her temple at Deshnoke is a place of pilgrimage to this day.

The tale the bards tell of their own calling begins on the morning of a battle. The legend does not name the king or the enemy, and it does not need to. It is a story that, the Charans say, happened many times in many places.

The army stood drawn up on the plain below the fort. The horses stamped in the cold air; the banners hung still. The king sat his horse at the head of his chiefs, and anyone close enough could see the doubt in his face. The enemy was strong. The scouts had brought bad news through the night. The king's chiefs waited for a word from him, and the word did not come.

"Can we win this day?" he asked at last, so quietly that only those nearest heard him.

No one answered. The silence spread back through the ranks like a chill.

Then the Charan stepped forward. He walked out in front of the army, where every man could see him, and turned to face the king. There was fire in his eyes.

"Maharaj," he said, "have you forgotten whose line you come from?"

The king looked down at him. For a moment, the chiefs held their breath. Few men would have dared to speak to a king so. But a Charan had both the right and the duty to say what others would not.

Then the Charan began to recite. He did not sing softly, as a man sings to himself. He raised his voice in the old measured cadence of Dingal verse, and the words rolled out over the ranks. He named the king's father and grandfather, and the great ancestors of his clan, one by one, and for each he named a battle where that ancestor had stood his ground.

"The blood that runs in your veins," he declaimed, "has never turned its back. The sword your fathers raised has never been lowered in shame. If you turn back today, the songs will not know your name."

It was not merely a poem. The bards say it was a fire, catching in every heart in turn. The soldiers straightened in their saddles. The chiefs looked at one another and gripped their weapons. And the king, the tradition says, felt the doubt go out of him like a breath. He drew his sword and raised it high. "We will not turn back!" he cried, and the army answered him with a roar.

Then the battle began. Horses charged, swords clashed, and the dust rose so thick that men fought half-blind. And the Charan did not withdraw to the safety of the fort. The tradition is clear on this: he stayed on the field. Charans did not usually fight, but they were expected to witness, and many of them stood close enough to the fighting to see every blow. Some, the histories record, died there.

As the battle raged, his voice rose above it. "See how this hero fights!" he cried, naming a warrior whose sword was already red. The man heard his name in the bard's mouth, and the bards say his spirit blazed higher still. "This war is not for land alone," the Charan called. "It is for honour!" And the ranks pressed forward.

A warrior fell close by. The Charan saw him go down, and at once his voice rose over the din. "He has not fallen," he declaimed. "He has become immortal." The fallen man's companions heard it, and they fought on with even greater fury, knowing that whatever happened, they too would be remembered.

The battle lasted for hours. When at last the dust settled, the field was covered with the dead of both sides. But there was something else on that field too, the bards say: a story, waiting to be told.

That night, by the fires, the Charan began to compose. He did not invent; his duty was to remember. He named the men who had fought and how they had fought, who had held the line and who had broken it, who had fallen and where. Those verses would be learned by his sons and by their sons, recited at weddings and funerals, at coronations and on the eve of new wars. In that way, an ordinary battle on an ordinary plain became part of the memory of a whole people.

Much of what we know of medieval Rajputana comes to us, in one form or another, through such voices. The great chronicles, the *khyats* and *vats*, drew on the songs and genealogies kept by bards. **Muhnot Nainsi**, the seventeenth-century minister of Marwar, gathered much of the material for his famous chronicle from oral traditions of this kind. The Charan poet **Dursa Adha** composed verses in praise of **Maharana Pratap** that are still recited, and tradition says he did not hesitate to praise Pratap's defiance even before the Mughal court. In the nineteenth century, **Suryamal Mishran** of Bundi wrote the vast *Vansh Bhaskar*, one of the last great works of the bardic tradition. Historians today read such sources with care, because praise poetry can exaggerate, but they could not tell the story of Rajputana without them.

The Charans were not only praise singers. They were the conscience of the court. When a king acted with honour, they made him immortal. When he acted with cowardice or broke his word, they made sure that too was remembered, and the Rajput dread of the bard's blame was as powerful as the hope of his praise. If a king wavered, it was they who steadied him. If a hero fell, it was they who gave him a second life in song.

Without them, perhaps the swords would still have fought, but the stories would have died with the men who carried them. The forts would stand as empty stone, and no one would know whose blood had been shed on their walls.

In the old forts of Rajasthan, guides still recite the verses the bards composed, and in the villages, old men still know couplets about heroes dead for five hundred years. People say that when the wind moves through the empty halls of a fort at evening, it sounds like a voice reciting. It is, perhaps, only the wind. But the Charans would say that it is the echo of their calling, and of the lesson they spent their lives teaching: that valour is not complete when it is won. It must also be remembered.

## Remembered for

- **Keepers of memory.** The Charans preserved the genealogies, deeds and sacrifices of the Rajput clans in Dingal verse, passing them from generation to generation.
- **The voice before battle.** Tradition tells of Charans steadying wavering kings and armies by reminding them of their ancestors.
- **Witnesses on the field.** Charans stood close to the fighting to see every deed, so that each warrior's part could be remembered.
- **Sacred and fearless.** Held to be inviolable, they acted as guarantors of oaths and protectors of caravans, and dared to rebuke even kings.
- **Karni Mata.** A Charan woman of the fifteenth century, revered by the Rathores of Bikaner, whose temple at Deshnoke is still a place of pilgrimage.
- **A living literature.** Poets such as Dursa Adha and Suryamal Mishran left works that remain among the great treasures of Rajasthani literature.
tale-of-the-charan-bards.coverAlt: A Charan bard reciting poetry in a royal court.

ballad-of-the-kesariya-turban.title: Ballad of the Kesariya Turban
ballad-of-the-kesariya-turban.hook: The color of the sun, the color of the final vow.
ballad-of-the-kesariya-turban.story:
## Ballad of the Kesariya Turban — the colour of the sun and of the final vow

*The saffron turban of the saka is not a legend but a real Rajput tradition, recorded in the histories of Chittor, Ranthambore, Jaisalmer and other besieged forts. The night told here is not one particular siege but the ballad the bards made of many; where it draws on history, and where on song, this story says so.*

The night was drawing its last breath. Torches flickered along the high walls of the fort, and a strange stillness hung in the air, the stillness that comes before a storm. Below the walls, as far as the eye could see in the dark, lay the camp of the besiegers: thousands of fires, the dark shapes of siege towers and battering engines, the endless murmur of a great army waiting for morning.

Inside the walls, there was no murmur at all. The siege had lasted for months. The granaries were nearly empty, and the great water tanks, which had seemed bottomless in the first weeks, were sinking. The garrison had beaten back assault after assault, but every assault had cost them men they could not replace. There would be no relief. Everyone in the fort knew it. And so, in that last night, a decision had been made, the oldest and hardest decision a Rajput fort could make.

History knows that decision by two names. For the women, it was **jauhar**: rather than fall into the hands of the conquerors, the queens and the women of the fort would give themselves to the fire. For the men, it was **saka**: dressed in saffron, they would open the gates and ride out to fight until not one of them remained. The bards tell of jauhar and saka at **Ranthambore** in **1301**, when **Hammir Dev Chauhan** fell defending his fort against **Alauddin Khalji**; at **Chittor** in **1303**, against the same sultan; at Chittor again in **1535**, against **Bahadur Shah** of Gujarat; and a third time at Chittor in **1568**, against the army of **Akbar**. Jaisalmer's own tradition speaks of its "two and a half sakas". The ballad of the kesariya turban is the song of all these nights at once.

The ballad imagines how that decision was reached. Earlier in the evening the chiefs had met in the hall of the palace, sitting on the bare floor because the carpets had long since been cut up for bandages. They spoke one after another, and no one spoke for long. Surrender was named only to be put aside: the terms the enemy offered meant captivity for the women and the loss of everything their fathers had held. A breakout by night had been tried and had failed. When the last voice had been heard, the eldest among them said simply that the time had come, and no one argued. Word was carried to the women's quarters, and the queens, the tradition says, had already reached their own decision before the messengers arrived.

In the courtyard of the fort, the warriors began to gather. No one shouted, and no one wept. There was only a deep, strange calm. In the middle of the courtyard, folded on a cloth, lay the saffron: bolts of cloth dyed the colour of the rising sun, the colour of fire, the colour that ascetics wear when they have given up the world. On a wedding day, a Rajput groom wore saffron too. On this night, the bards say, the warriors were going to a wedding with death.

An old chief stepped forward first. His beard was white and his hands were scarred from forty years of war. He lifted a length of saffron cloth and, for a long moment, simply looked at it, as if he could see his whole life in its folds: his boyhood in the hills, his first battle, his sons, the lord he had served. Then, slowly and carefully, he wound it around his head into a turban.

The tradition says that in that moment he changed. He was no longer only a man. He was a vow.

One by one, the others followed. A father tied on the saffron and looked across the courtyard at his son doing the same. Brothers helped each other tie the knots. Old friends, who had quarrelled and made peace a dozen times over the years, stood side by side and said nothing, because words were no longer enough.

A young warrior came forward. He was barely more than a boy, and his hands were trembling. He held the saffron cloth but did not tie it.

"Will we... not come back?" he asked softly.

The old chief looked at him. There was compassion in his eyes, but there was also a hard truth, and he would not hide it.

"We will come back," he said. "But not in these bodies. We will come back as a story. Every time someone in this land ties on the saffron, we will be standing beside him."

For a moment the young man's breath stopped. Then he lifted the cloth, wound it around his head, and stood straight.

Above them, behind the inner walls, a glow was rising into the sky. The fire of the jauhar had been lit. The bards never describe that fire directly. They speak of the glow, of the silence that fell over the courtyard as the men turned to watch it, of the knowledge that their mothers, wives, sisters and daughters had chosen their own end rather than captivity. To modern hearts the jauhar is a terrible thing to contemplate, and so it was to those who lived it. The ballads remember it not as glory alone but as the grief that made the saka inevitable. Now nothing remained behind them. There was no one left to defend, no home to return to. There was only the gate, and what lay beyond it.

The horses were brought to the gate, saddled and ready. The men mounted. Swords were drawn and caught the torchlight. The old chief rode to the front and turned to face them.

"Today," he called, "none of us returns alive!"

And from hundreds of throats the answer came back, echoing off the stones and up into the sky: "**Har Har Mahadev!**"

Slowly, with a groan of old timber and iron, the great gates began to swing open. Outside, the besieging army was stirring in the grey light, unaware for a moment of what was coming. Inside, death was ready. And between the two, in a column of saffron, rode the warriors.

The first horse stepped out through the gate. Then all of them charged.

The bards make the next hour into a long, rolling verse. They sing of horses running flat out down the slope, of swords flashing, of a storm of dust rising around the saffron turbans so that they seemed to burn in it. Every warrior fought as though he were the last; no one looked back, because behind them there was nothing left.

One warrior was struck by an arrow and fell. He rose again, bleeding, and shouted, "Not yet!" and threw himself back into the fight. Another was thrown from his horse, and from the ground he went on swinging his sword. The enemy, which had expected to walk into a starving fort, found itself facing men who had already given up their lives and had nothing left to lose. It was not a battle, the bards say. It was a final dance.

Somewhere in the thick of it, the ballad finds the young warrior again. His hands are no longer trembling. He has lost his horse and fights on foot beside the old chief, guarding the old man's side as the old man guards his. For a little while the two of them hold a narrow space among the enemy, back to back, the saffron on their heads the only bright thing in the dust. Then the old chief falls, and the young man stands over him and fights until he too goes down. The bards do not give them names. They say only that the boy who had asked whether they would come back had his answer.

One by one, the saffron turbans fell. But with each one, the enemy lost men too. History records that the besiegers of these forts paid dearly for every one of their victories. Blood mingled with the dust. And as the sun cleared the horizon, a silence fell over the ground outside the walls.

The enemy stood there. It had won; the fort was open. But, the ballad says, for a long while it could not bring itself to advance. It had seen what it had fought. It was not merely a garrison. It was defiance, and a message that would be carried back through every camp and every court: that there were people who could be killed, but not made to bow.

History is less tender than the ballads, and conquerors did enter these forts. At Chittor in 1568, Akbar's army took the fort and great slaughter followed. But the memory of the saka outlived every victory. The walls of Chittor still stand above the plain, and the bards say the colour of that dawn still hangs in the air around them.

Even today, when a Rajput ties on a kesariya turban, at a wedding, at a festival, or on a day of remembrance, it is not just a piece of cloth. It is a memory, and an oath. The bards sing that it carries the faith of those who rode out of the gate: that when the darkness is deepest, the brightest fire burns.

Saffron is the colour that does not fear death. It is the colour that says: life may end, but honour, never.

## Remembered for

- **The colour of the vow.** Saffron, the colour of fire, of renunciation and of the bridegroom, was worn by warriors who rode out to fight to the last.
- **Jauhar and saka.** The women of a doomed fort chose the fire of jauhar; the men, in saffron, opened the gates for the final charge of the saka.
- **Ranthambore, 1301.** Hammir Dev Chauhan's last stand against Alauddin Khalji is among the earliest sakas remembered by the bards.
- **The three sakas of Chittor.** Chittor saw jauhar and saka in 1303, 1535 and 1568, against Alauddin Khalji, Bahadur Shah and Akbar.
- **"Har Har Mahadev."** The war cry with which the saffron-clad warriors rode out through the gates.
- **A living tradition.** The kesariya turban is still worn at weddings and on days of remembrance across Rajasthan.
ballad-of-the-kesariya-turban.coverAlt: Rajput warriors tying saffron turbans before battle.

legend-of-the-rajput-sword-oath.title: Legend of the Rajput Sword Oath
legend-of-the-rajput-sword-oath.hook: A promise etched in steel and sealed with blood.
legend-of-the-rajput-sword-oath.story:
## Legend of the Rajput Sword Oath — a promise etched in steel

*This is a village legend, told across the desert country of western Rajasthan in many forms and with many names, or with none. It cannot be tied to a single place or year. It is set here against the real customs of the Rajput sword and the real tradition of the village guardian heroes; where the tale is legend, this story says so.*

The first line of dawn had only just appeared on the horizon when the dust began to rise. Far out across the waves of sand, beyond the last thorn trees and the last field walls, a brown haze lifted into the pale sky, and with it, faint at first, came the sound of hooves.

In the village, people stopped what they were doing. A woman at the well set down her pot. An old man drawing water let the rope go slack. They knew that sound, and they knew that dust. It was not a merchant's caravan or a wedding party. It was raiders.

In the desert country of medieval Rajputana, such mornings were a real and familiar terror. Between the great kingdoms lay wide stretches of sand where the authority of any ruler was thin, and bands of mounted raiders lived by striking at villages, driving off cattle and carrying away grain. A village had little to defend itself with: a low mud wall, a gate of thorn and timber, a few old weapons, and whatever courage its people could find.

That morning, the tellers say, this village had one thing more. It had a young Rajput, the son of the village's landholding family, who stood in the lane outside his father's house with a sword in his hand. The legend gives him no name, or rather it gives him a different name in every village where it is told, because every village claims him as its own. He was young, and that morning he was alone, for his father had died the winter before and his elder kinsmen had ridden away to serve their lord in a distant war.

The sword was not new. Its blade was dark with age and its hilt was worn smooth by the hands of many generations. The tellers say that it was older than the village wall, older than the well, older than anyone's memory. Among the Rajputs a sword was never only a weapon. On the festival of **Dussehra** it was taken down, cleaned and worshipped in the ceremony of *shastra puja*, honoured as an image of the goddess's power. At a wedding, if a groom could not be present, his sword could stand in his place, and the bride would be married to the blade. Oaths were sworn with a hand on the hilt. To break such an oath was to dishonour not only oneself but every hand that had ever held that sword.

He remembered the day it had been given to him. He had been a boy of twelve, and his father had placed the sword across his two open palms. "This is not only a weapon," his father had said. "It is your word. Whatever you swear upon it, you must keep, even if it costs you everything." The boy had closed his small hands around the hilt and said, as solemnly as he could, "I will keep its honour." His father had smiled, and had said nothing more.

Now that day had come.

The villagers gathered around him in the lane, frightened, all speaking at once. The raiders were many; the scouts on the dunes had counted more horsemen than the village had men. "What shall we do?" an old man asked at last, and the crowd fell silent to hear the answer.

The young man drew the sword from its scabbard. The first ray of the sun fell on the blade and it seemed to blaze.

"We will fight," he said.

"But there are so many of them," someone said.

"I am here," he answered.

For a moment there was silence. Then he took the hilt in both hands, closed his eyes, and raised the blade before his face. When he spoke, his voice carried down the lane and over the wall.

"I swear on this sword: as long as it is in my hand, this village will not fall."

The tellers say those words were not just words. They were a bond, as binding as any made before a temple or a Charan. Some of the village men came to stand beside him. Some, ashamed and afraid, drew back. He did not blame them. He only turned towards the gate.

They did what they could. The women and children were sent into the strongest house at the centre of the village. The cattle were driven into the lanes behind it. Thorn branches were piled against the weakest parts of the wall. The few men who had bows climbed onto the roofs. "Close the gate!" someone shouted, and the flimsy gate was dragged shut and barred.

The young man climbed onto the wall and watched the riders come. Now he could see them clearly: lean men on hard desert horses, faces wrapped against the dust, spears and swords glinting. Their leader rode in front, a big man on a grey horse. "Remember," the young man said to the men beside him, "behind us is our home."

The first rush struck the gate. The raiders crashed against it, shoving and shouting, hacking at the timber. From the roofs the arrows began to fly. Some of the raiders fell; the rest did not stop. "Break it!" their leader roared. The gate shuddered, and shuddered again, and the bar began to crack.

The young man came down from the wall and stood in the lane behind the gate, the sword gripped tight in both hands. "Now," he said quietly.

The gate burst open, and the raiders poured through.

The first man through the gap fell to his sword. So did the second, and the third. In the narrow lane the raiders could not use their numbers, and he fought them as they came, one after another. There was no fear in his movements, the tellers say, only resolve. A spear drove into his arm. He tore it out and fought on. "Don't fall back!" he shouted to the men around him.

But one by one his companions fell, or broke and fled. At last he stood almost alone in the lane, with the raiders all around him and the dead at his feet. Their leader rode forward on his grey horse and looked down at him, laughing.

"What will you do now?" he said.

The young man did not answer him. He raised the sword. "As long as I stand," he said, "you will not pass."

Then he charged. Raider after raider fell before him, but his wounds were mounting, and his breath came harder with every stroke. Blood ran down his arm and over the old hilt. Still his hands held the sword.

"Why do you fight?" one of the raiders shouted at him, half in anger and half in wonder. "You cannot win."

"Because I gave my word," he said.

He struck one last blow, and one more enemy fell. Then his knees gave way and he sank down into the dust of the lane. But his sword arm was still raised, the blade still pointing at the men before him.

The raiders stopped. They looked at one another. Behind the fallen young man, the lane was still barred by the dead of their own band, and further on, they could hear the village men gathering again on the rooftops. "He is mad," one of them muttered. But none of them stepped forward. After a few moments their leader wheeled his grey horse around, and the raiders rode out of the broken gate and away into the dunes, leaving the cattle and the grain behind.

The village was saved.

When the sun had fully risen, the people came out into the lane. They found him lying where he had fallen, at peace, his face turned towards the gate. His fingers were still closed around the hilt of the sword, so tightly that the tellers say no one could loosen them, as though the promise were still alive in his hand.

Across Rajasthan, real villages honour heroes like him. A man who died defending a village, its land or its cattle was often remembered as a **bhomiya**, a guardian spirit of the place, and a memorial stone carved with a mounted warrior was set up where he fell. Villagers still offer lamps and flowers at such stones. The great folk epics of the region tell the same story on a grander scale. The bards of the *Pabuji ri Phad* sing of **Pabuji Rathore**, who, the epic says, rose from his own wedding to keep his promise to protect a Charan woman's cattle, and died fighting the raiders who had taken them. The legend of the sword oath belongs to this same tradition, where keeping one's word mattered more than keeping one's life.

The tellers end the tale in the same way everywhere. When a Rajput raises a sword, they say, he does not raise only a weapon. He takes up an oath. In Rajputana, words were like swords: once drawn, they were not put back. And it was that promise, kept to the last breath, that made an ordinary young man of an ordinary village into someone who would never be forgotten.

## Remembered for

- **The oath on the hilt.** Tradition says he swore on his ancestral sword that the village would not fall while he held it.
- **The father's words.** He kept the lesson he had been given as a boy: that a sword is a man's word, and must be kept whatever it costs.
- **Holding the lane.** When the gate broke, he fought the raiders alone in the narrow lane until they turned back.
- **The grip that would not open.** The tale says his fingers were still closed around the hilt when the villagers found him.
- **The guardian heroes.** His legend belongs to the tradition of the bhomiyas, village heroes honoured with memorial stones across Rajasthan.
- **The spirit of Pabuji.** It echoes the folk epic of Pabuji Rathore, who died keeping his promise to protect a Charan woman's cattle.
legend-of-the-rajput-sword-oath.coverAlt: A warrior taking a solemn oath over his sword.

tale-of-the-desert-falcon.title: Tale of the Desert Falcon
tale-of-the-desert-falcon.hook: Eyes that saw through the sandstorm, heart that never faltered.
tale-of-the-desert-falcon.story:
## Tale of the Desert Falcon — the scout who rode through the storm

*The tale of Maru Baaz, the Falcon of the Desert, is a folk legend of the Thar. No chronicle records his real name, his fort or his year, and the tellers do not claim that it does. It is set here against the real life of the desert and its watchers; where the story is legend, it says so.*

The desert was not calm that day. Since noon the sky had been turning yellow, then a dull and angry orange, and the wind had changed its nature. It was no longer blowing; it was roaring. Grains of sand rose off the dunes and gathered into a moving wall that could blind the eyes and choke the breath. Herders on the plains had already driven their flocks into the lee of the rocks and wrapped their faces in cloth. Anyone in the Thar knew what was coming. It was an *aandhi*, a sandstorm.

And somewhere inside that storm, the tellers say, a shadow was riding.

His name is not written in any history. The people of the desert knew him by only one name, **Maru Baaz**, the Falcon of the Desert. The name was a title of affection and of respect, the kind of name that ordinary people give to someone whose real name hardly matters any more, because what he does matters more.

He had been different from childhood. In the long summers of the Thar, when the other children kept to the shade of the houses through the burning afternoons, he ran barefoot across the dunes. When travellers lost their way among the shifting sand, he could find the path. His eyes, the tellers say, could see a rider on the horizon before anyone else in the village knew there was anything there. And he seemed to understand the desert as if it were a language.

In this he was not alone, and the legend draws on something real. The people of the Thar have always had their watchers and readers of the land. Their trackers, the *pagis* or *khojis*, could follow a man or a camel across miles of sand by his footprints, telling how heavily he was loaded and how tired he was, and such skills are still valued in the desert today. Herders read the wind and the clouds and knew where the wells lay buried under drifted sand. In a land where a wrong turn could mean death by thirst, knowledge of the desert was itself a kind of wealth.

The boy learned all of this from an old man of the village, a tracker who had served the fort in his youth. "The sand speaks," the old man told him once, sitting on a dune at sunset and letting a handful of it run through his fingers. "Every grain is moving somewhere. The wind writes on the dunes all day long. You only have to learn to read it."

After years of training, the boy was no longer just a soldier when he entered the service of the fort. He became something else: a shadow on the border. His work was not to fight in the front rank, but to ride alone at the edges of the kingdom, to watch, to listen, and to warn the fort before it was too late. The great desert forts of the Thar, like **Jaisalmer**, raised by **Rawal Jaisal** of the Bhati Rajputs in the twelfth century on its ridge of golden stone, stood in a country where an enemy could appear out of the open sand with little warning. Their safety depended on such watchers far more than on any song about them.

One day, the tale says, he was out on the border, alone, standing on a high dune with his horse beside him. The morning was quiet and the wind was normal. Everything was calm. And then, far off, very far off, he saw something that was not right. It was a faint ripple of dust, moving against the wind.

His eyes narrowed. "That is not the wind," he murmured. Dust that moves with the wind is the desert's own. Dust that moves against it is raised by hooves.

He watched for a long time. Then he saw a glint, the flash of sunlight on metal, and then another, and then many. As the distance closed he could make out the dark line beneath the dust: horsemen, more than he could count, riding steadily towards the fort. They were coming by a route that the fort did not expect, through a stretch of open desert that was thought to be too dry and too far for an army to cross.

There was very little time. He leapt into the saddle. "Go!" he said, and the horse sprang forward down the face of the dune.

But just then the sky changed. The air grew heavy and still, and then, out of the west, the storm came down on him.

In a moment the world vanished. There was sand on every side, sand in the air, sand in his eyes and his mouth. The sun disappeared. The tracks he had been following were wiped away, and the dunes he knew became strange shapes in the howling dark. His horse staggered and shied. "Don't stop," he told it, and urged it forward.

Breathing was hard now, and seeing was impossible. So, the tellers say, he stopped trying to see. He shut his eyes and felt instead: the direction of the wind on his cheek, the slope of the ground beneath the horse's hooves, the hiss of the sand as it flowed over the crest of a dune. He remembered the old tracker's words. The sand speaks.

"Left," he whispered, and the horse turned. A while later, he stopped again and listened. "No. Right." He was not seeing his way; he was hearing it. The desert, the tellers say, was speaking to him.

It felt as though hours had passed. The storm only grew fiercer. Once, on a steep slope, the horse lost its footing, and both of them went down, rolling in the soft sand. For a moment everything was still, and the sand began to drift over them. Then he got up. He pulled the horse to its feet, held its head between his hands and looked into its eyes. "Not yet," he said. And the two of them ran on.

Slowly, the storm began to die down. The roaring sank to a moan, then to a whisper. The yellow light came back. And there, ahead of him in the distance, was the fort on its ridge. But behind him, he knew, the enemy was coming too, and now that the storm was passing, nothing would slow them.

He rode one last time with all the strength that was left in him and his horse. At the gate the sentries saw a figure covered in sand come out of the haze and raised their spears. "Who goes there?" they shouted.

He did not stop. "Open the gate!" he cried. "The enemy is coming!"

In an instant the alarm was raised. Drums began to beat along the walls. The fort woke as if from sleep. "Call the men to the walls!" "Shut the outer gates!" "Bring the archers up!" Within moments the fort was ready for battle.

He slid from the saddle, his breath coming in great gasps. A chief came hurrying down to meet him. "How far?" he asked.

"Only a little while," the Falcon said.

And as if in answer, on the horizon, the dust of the approaching army appeared.

The battle that followed is told briefly in the legend, because it is not the heart of the story. The enemy had counted on surprise, and it found the gates shut, the walls manned and the defenders waiting. Its plan had failed before it began. The attack was fierce, but the walls held, and in the end the enemy fell back into the desert it had come from.

When the sun rose on the next day, the fort was safe. People in the town below came out of their houses and breathed again. But the Falcon himself, the tellers say, was silent. He stood alone on the rampart, his eyes still fixed on the far horizon, as if he were already watching for the next danger.

"You saved us," the chief said, coming to stand beside him.

He only nodded. "It was my duty."

There were no cheers for him and no celebration. That was the nature of his work: it was never seen. When a scout did his job well, nothing happened, and no one sings songs about nothing happening. Yet that unseen work was what kept the kingdom alive.

Even today, the people of the Thar say, when the wind blows hard across the dunes and the sand runs in long ribbons over their crests, it sometimes looks as though a shadow were riding through it. They call it Maru Baaz, the warrior who was never seen, but because of whom the forts still stand.

## Remembered for

- **The Falcon of the Desert.** Tradition knows him only as Maru Baaz, a scout whose real name the desert has forgotten.
- **Reading the sand.** He learned from an old tracker that "the sand speaks", the skill of the real pagis and khojis of the Thar.
- **Dust against the wind.** He saw that a ripple of dust moving against the wind could only mean horsemen.
- **Riding blind through the storm.** In the sandstorm, the tale says, he found his way by feeling the wind and listening to the sand.
- **The warning in time.** He reached the fort just before the enemy, so that the gates were shut and the walls manned.
- **The unseen hero.** He asked for no reward, and is remembered for the quiet work that kept the forts of the desert standing.
